description: An employee or contractor to AllRig (a direct contractor to Seadrill), died while performing work on the Seadrill West Neptune drilling unit, which at the time was under contract to Kosmos Energy Gulf of Mexico Operations, LLC ("Kosmos") for operations on Kosmos' Kodiak 3 well. Investigations are ongoing, both by the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement as well as an investigation by Seadrill in which Kosmos is participating. We understand AllRig may be conducting its own investigation. Subject in all respects to the final investigative report to be issued by Seadrill and Kosmos, below is information that Kosmos has received from Seadrill and which was extracted from an HSE alert sent by Seadrill to its fleet. The wording may vary somewhat from that alert. On January 24th, 2021 at approximately 13:30 Central Time, two AllRig personnel were performing loose lifting gear inspections on and around the riser deck area of the Seadrill West Neptune. The task was to visually inspect slings. During the inspection, the inspection team leader observed two steel slings wrapped around a bundle of 5 metal plates which were stacked vertically, resting on dunnage, and secured to a stanchion by a single 2" ratchet strap. The slings had been left in place on the plates after they were landed by the crane for efficiency and ease of relocation when needed. The plates all measured 4 x 8 feet; three (3) were 3/8" thick and two (2) were 1" thick weighing a combined 1.8T (3,600lbs). The inspection team leader was successful in sliding one of the slings from the plates on the inboard side of the plates, but he discovered the second sling was pinched between the rear of the plates and the stanchion, preventing it from being taken off on the outboard side. He then called his assistant to help free the sling and remove it for inspection. The lead inspector instructed the assistant to 'loosen' the ratchet strap. It is assumed that the inspection team leader thought that loosening the rachet strap would provide the opportunity to move the trapped sling. Prior to instructing the assistant to loosen the ratchet strap, the inspection team leader leaned his back against the plates. The reason for this is unknown, but it is assumed the intention was to support the plates in their standing position when the ratchet strap was loosened. Directly in front of the lead inspector was the framework of the drilling bail rack. When the ratchet strap was manipulated by the assistant, the ratchet strap hook released from the stanchion allowing the plates to free fall forward (away from the stanchion) under their own weight, fatally trapping the inspection team leader between the plates and the framework of the drilling bail rack.

description: Operators were using the personnel basket to move several Glycol Charcoal Filters from inside the NW Hull Column to an area on the NW Main Deck. When the basket swung near (and about 15-20' above) the Booster Compressor #1 Exhaust; the wind pushed the basket over the exhaust. Once the basket came within close proximity to the (approximately) 1,200 °F exhaust; the ropes holding the personnel basket platform began to melt. Initial Actions Taken: -The riggers told the Crane Operator to finish booming down and land the load as quickly as possible. Follow-Up Actions Taken: -Once the load was safely on deck; the Operators inspected the personnel basked. -The Ropes securing the personnel basket's platform tarp had melted through on one side, so the basket was placed out of service. -To ensure that it is not used; the Operators attached an OOS Tag to the Personnel Basket's Upper Master Link. Response to RFI: *Why did they use a personnel basket vs utility/equipment basket? -They did not think about using the cargo basket. (Complacency) Note: Both the OIM and our HSE Team Lead discussed this with everyone involved and the rest of the crew, so this does not occur again. Recommendations from Incident Investigation: -Contractors to review the (HSE.GOM.PRG-06.014) Personnel Basket Transfer Program and the (HSE.GOM.PRG-06.11) Crane Operation Program and amend the Crane Operations JSA to include requirements in relation to cargo transfers. -Also consider identifying the high temperature Booster Compressor Exhausts as a hazard on the JSA. -There is a "no fly / no lift" zone within a 30'-0" radius of the (approx. 1,200 °F) Booster Compressor #1 & #2 exhaust stacks.

description: During the process of cutting and proving well: While pulling the IMCT (Internal Multi-string Cutting Tool) out of the well with the umbilical; located on the pipe deck and operated by a technician. During the hoisting operation, the Launch and Recovery System (LARS) and Proving Frame Assembly, became dislodged from the base cross beams, The LARS and Proving Frame was displaced, coming to rest at an angle, on the box girders and box girders crossbeam. No personnel were in the area of the LARS nor in the well bay and no injuries occurred to personnel. Immediate Corrective Actions: Work was stopped to assess the equipment; BSEE was notified by e-Mail and after hours phone of the incident by FMOG management, danger tape the affected area and instruct personnel to stay clear of the equipment. Investigation Results: Changes made to operation/design without use of contractor's MoC process, availability of hydraulic pressure indication for umbilical reel operator was unknown by operator, no shut-off or alarm for operator of an overpull situation, pressure set-points for hydraulic motors was not verified prior to start of task onsite, and set-points were found to be out of range. Reel operator was an SSE. SSEs onsite was not communicated to FMOG. All personnel had safety training, but SSEs lacked operational training/experience for task. Project specs and equipment were different (larger/bigger/heavier) than previous projects performed by contractor. Did not take into account increased lateral loads in design of installation. Contractor did not utilize SWA when it was identified they did not have adequate personnel for project. Recurrence Prevention Corrective Actions: -Action 1 - Administrative -Update planning process so that client provided sea-fastening is verified by internal engineering team. -Action 2 - Administrative / Training -Familiarize the operations team with the latest Project Management Process. -Required reading will be assigned and monitored to completion. -MOC Training for the team. -Stop Work Authority Training -Action 3 - Potential Engineered Improvement -Bolt options for fastening the LARS & proving frame. -Action 4 - SPAC (Standard Policies Administrative Controls). -OMM Procedures will be updated to have a verification step for the set pressure at which the winch will not be able to pull greater than the pre-determined amount. This will be verified during FAT and at the jobsite. FM O&G -Add language from SSE policy to MSC instead of referencing all policies Per Oceaneering: . LARS: 6700 pounds . IMCT Packer: 475 pounds . description: Evacuation of personnel due to facility loss of power. Platform life safety systems were being powered initially by a primary 500 KW NOV rental generator. At 3:00 P.M., the rental generator went down. The platform's Emergency Generator was put online and ran for 1 hour before the mechanic manually shut down it down due to critical mechanical/electrical concerns. The primary rental generator issue was trouble shot during the time the Emergency Generator was online. The issue was initially identified as a control board malfunction and replacement part ordered. The part was sent out but the crew ran out of time to repair due to daylight and transportation availability. At that time, the Production Superintendent was notified that the facility was completely without power. The platform was secured and unmanned and the personnel transported to the facility for housing. The crew was not able to return to the Spar facility due to inclement weather until 2/18/2021. Upon return, a technician came out with extra parts to help troubleshoot and repair the primary 500 KW rental generator. The problem with the rental generator was found to be broken wires on the wiring harness to the control board. Once the wiring harness was replaced, the rental generator was put back on line. The platform Emergency Generator was trouble shot and determined that the generator's PMG wiring had failed. A second rental generator was procured for the platform and the Emergency Generator was placed permanently out of service. Power for the facility is now being supplied by the primary 500 KW NOV rental generator and a back up 350 KW NOV rental generator.

description: The team reported a strong sour odor throughout the production deck downwind of the float cell. Email correspondence attached including follow up correspondence on wellhead and 22".

description: At approximately 1655 hours local time on April 24, 2021, well abandonment personnel speared into the 18-5/8" casing on the C-4 well at the wellhead deck. The well abandonment team was attempting to start pulling and laying down the C-4 conductor. The top of conductor was at the mezzanine deck where a 9-inch pin hole was drilled. The team continued to lift the C-4 conductor to begin pinning operations. At 39.5-ft lift height, the 24-inch conductor separated from the 18-5/8" casing, likely from either poor cement bond in the 18-5/8" x 24" casing annulus or there was no cement behind pipe. The 24"conductor then slid down the 18-5/8" casing until it reached origination height at the well head deck. When the 24" conductor came to a stop at its originating spot, the descent broke the welds on the pollution ring. Three members of the well abandonment team were on the mezzanine deck where they had just completed drilling the 9" pin holes in the C-4 conductor, which consisted of the 18-5/8" casing and 24" conductor. Each were standing a safe distance, approximately 20', from the conductor that was being lifted. One heard a "rush of air", one heard a "loud sound" and the third heard "two metal objects hitting." At which time they saw the 24" conductor descending at a high rate of speed. All three personnel headed toward the egress point running. One team member slipped during the expedited egress resulting in a minor abrasion below the knee. It is worth noting that March 26, 2021, FM O&G verified the mechanical cut at 20' BML by picking up the C-4 conductor, 4' at 191,000 lbs. and set the conductor back down. The operation was performed using the same 18-5/8" casing spear that picked up the C-4 conductor on April 24, 2021. Immediate Corrective Actions: The area around the well slot was barricaded until an assessment could be completed. It was determined that the 24" conductor had safely landing in its pre-pull position. The 18-5/8" Casing was secure and hanging from the spear assembly. Some grating will need to be repaired on the mezzanine deck. During the night and continuing today, the 18-5/8" casing is being pulled. Once on deck, it will be examined for cement pumped during the original well completion. Investigation Results: 18-5/8" casing was not completely cemented above the mudline as was indicated in the well completion report. This lack of adhesion between the two pipes allowed the 24" conductor to separate from the casing when lifted with the casing spear. It was also discovered after the event; the casing head was a gravity type and not traditional. This information was not on the completion report. Recurrence Prevention: On the platform we will be utilizing the proving clamp on all wells. The reason the clamp was not utilized in the incident is that a casing spear was used on traditional casing heads. So going forward an observation and evaluation is being completed before lifting the casing head to determine which type casing head it is. If the casing head is gravity held a proving clamp will be used and a 4" pin will be put into place before the casing head is cut to prevent any of the casing heads after being cut from falling off. If it is a traditional casing head it will be speared with casing spear, if possible, and we cannot get the proving clamp on the conductor.

description: On 05-05-2021 the M/V HOS Captain was conducting cargo operations at MC 37. While utilizing the rig's crane, a frame being lifted from the deck of the M/V HOS Captain came in contact with the IP. No medical attention was requested and the AB continued to perform their job duties. At the time of the incident the vessel reported their VSat communications was being blocked and stated this to be the reason for the late reporting. The Ocean Blackhawk was not notified the incident had occurred until the evening of 05-07-2021. Update 5-19-2021: The following activities led up to the event: The rig crane operator positioned the rig crane and lowered the hook to prepare for the load. The senior AB (AB1/Mentor) advised a Short Service Employee Ordinary Seaman (OS/Mentee) to temporarily hold the hook while a tagline was being clipped in. AB1 knelt on the deck to attach the tagline to the underside of the metal frame. While the tagline was being attached, the OS clipped the crane hook to the D-ring which was attached to a four-part sling on the frame, making the load "live". While AB1 was still kneeling on the deck, the vessel rolled, causing the "live" load to shift slightly and strike AB1. The root cause identified from Hornbeck's investigation were Inadequate hazard assessment - The JSA was completed at the beginning of the crews' watch and was "generic" to deck cargo. The hazards and risks of each specific lift were not considered. Therefore, the crew did not consider that the tagline needed to be attached to the frame prior to the crane hook being lowered into position. Corrective actions include (1) The crew did not consider the relative movement of the vessel to be a hazard to the load with the hook connected but the drillship crane not actively engaged (2) This event occurred after a 14-hour transit to the worksite in weather conditions that prevented the crew from resting fully. Corrective action: Hornbeck launched a fleet-wide training module on risk identification including threat controls and the accurate generation of risk tools.

description: Operators identified wiring on battery bank that had begun to smolder / melt the coating upon turning on battery power to check Diesel Generator for operation. Power was immediately shut off to Generator and it was not running at the time. The Field Electrician was called, and opened the panel door, found the wiring starting to smoke and then a small 2" flame ignited. Cut the negative ground wire going to the battery and the flame ceased. There were no injuries or further damage except the 3 wires coming from battery. ROOT CAUSE: Initial findings: . Initially found wires from the battery burnt. The negative wire was burnt from the battery to ground terminal in the panel. Also found other wires that had pieces of the coating melted from being close to the above mentioned negative wire. . Possible cause: High amp draw during start-up. Repairs made: . Changed out the wires from the batteries. Spliced additional wires that had parts of the coat melted. . All wires affected or damaged were changed in its entirety. Conclusion . Checked the amp draw that was coming from the starter to verify what it was reading. . With the generator running the amp draw was at a 2, and with it not running it's also at a 2. . Once personnel attempt to crank the generator the amp draw shoots up to a 28amp. . Currently awaiting a confirmation from electrical foreman on what the engine starter is supposed to be using when attempting to crank. INVESTIGATION & CORRECTIVE ACTIONS: We have confirmed with a volt meter that the DC Voltage when read from the positive side of the battery to the negative post is slightly different than the reading from positive side to panel chassis ground. This is fairly common when grounding is done at different locations. This would indicate that there are different ground potentials based on the distance from the battery negative and the materials resistance (steel and copper wire) between battery negative and grounding location. There is a possibility before the technicians cleaned up the connections on the main feeder grounds, the panel became part of the return circuit for the starter, which burned the original wiring. With a fuse in place of the original ground block in the panel, the wire is now protected in the event that the starter circuit was to have a ground issue and use the chassis for return.

description: At approximately 6:45 pm operators and other facility personnel smelled smoke on the production deck. Lead Operator conducted on site investigation to identify the source and discovered the Instrument Air After Cooler was emitting smoke with visible flame coming out of the top of the unit. Additionally, the piping on the suction for the Air Cooler was smoldering from charred paint with evidence of intense heat. Power to the unit was shut off and the fire extinguished with portable extinguishers and a fire hose. Root Cause: An investigation to determine the cause of this fire was initiated. Samples of liquids and residuals from the air compression system were gathered at the following key points: Cooler suction, cooler discharge, pipe inlet to cooler, and air cooler. Samples were analyzed to determine the qualitative constituency and flammability. While no sample at or upstream of the fire exhibited potential fuel content, pyrophoric properties, nor flammability, it is suspected that potential hydrocarbon content from lube oil built up over time in a low spot in the header pipe from the discharge of the air compressors. It is also suspected that heat of compression at the discharge of the air compressors may have allowed for conditions to ignite the residual material within the pipe (i.e., presence of fuel source, oxygen, and heat) without any indication of a pyrophoric event. This was tentatively confirmed with the presence of deposits in the air cooler, downstream of the fire location, that exhibited flammability potential. Corrective Action: The affected suction and header piping and other nearby equipment affected by heat or flame will be replaced. Additional equipment will be installed to allow operators to drain any buildup of lube oils or other residuals to avoid any similar occurrence.

description: Contractor Supervisor: Jerad Moneaux On 8/23/2021 @ approximately 1700 while preparing the SS253-F platform for Decommissioning, EcoServe employee Jean Paul Mouton, a tank / vessel cleaning technician, was directed by his supervisor to start draining pressure from the 2" Meter Run Piping of the Gas Lift Header (GAS #4459) on the cellar deck of the platform. The employee located the blind flange on the header with a 1" ball valve containing a 1" plug. The line was 15-18' long with a block valve on one end and several needle valves. The block valve was closed with apparent pressure trapped from the valve to the blind which was unknown to the employee who open the valve without first checking for and bleeding off pressure under control of the needle valve. When the employee opened the valve trapped pressure released onto the sleeve of his cover-all contacting his left forearm and hand. The employee sustained redness to the skin surface and was subsequently brought to shore for medical elevation. Employee was evacuated to shore on 8/23/21 at approximately 10:00PM. Employee was on the 4th day of a 14 day hitch. Fieldwood Energy is investigating in conjunction with EcoServe HSE and will report contributing causes and corrective actions accordingly. 8/25/2021 UPDATE: Ecoserv employee was evaluated at Gulf Regional Occ/Med Center and diagnosed with minor skin abrasion / redness (1st Aid) and released immediately to full duty / no restrictions. Based on the investigation and post incident interviews the following are writings specific to the root cause of the impactful event and provide prevention guidance to avoid such occurrences in the future. Root Cause: The involved parties failed to identify PRIMARY and SECONDARY pressure relief controls and prior opening a discharge control device the internal pressure was not verified at a zero-energy state. A) Primary pressure relief - Needle Valve used within the fluid processing or flow metering application as a device suited for pressure control. B)Secondary pressure relief - 1" Ball Valve used within the fluid processing or flow metering application as a device to control fluid or flow, thus not intended to depressurize to atmosphere. Process Approach and Prevention Focus: 1) All pressures must be verified at a zero state before opening any discharge or access point of installed piping or a vessel. 2) Personnel opening discharge or access points must assume lines and/or valves are pressurized and contain liquids, therefore adequate secondary containment shall be in place and NO portion of one's body shall be positioned in a line of fire position.

description: October 2, 2021: during a line ride, an oil sheen was detected off the coastline and reported to the platform personnel at approximately 8:00 am PT. Upon notification of the oil sheen, platform personnel initiated the Oil Spill Response Plan and notified regulatory agencies. On October 3, it was announced that a Unified Command was established to respond to the oil spill. The cause, timing, and details regarding the spill are currently being investigated and this information is preliminary. Cause Update, 3-17-22: During a large winter storm on January 25, 2021, the two supertankers were driven by winds and waves and drug their anchors across the seafloor and into areas where federal law prohibits anchoring. As the two supertankers dragged their anchors, both anchors hooked onto the concrete-encased pipeline and dragged a 4,000-foot section of the pipeline across the seafloor. The anchor-dragging bent and bowed the pipeline, displacing some parts of the pipeline by more than 100 feet and breaking off the concrete casing around the pipeline. Neither vessel nor the Marine Exchange of Southern California, responsible for managing ship positions in the harbor, informed anyone at Beta or Amplify that there was an anchor dragging incident across the exclusion zone. Timing Update 3-17-22: Over the course of the later afternoon and evening of October 1, the offshore platform and onshore pipeline personnel worked together to troubleshoot and rectify what were believed to be false leak detection system alarms. Following each alarm, the crews investigated various components of the platform and the pipeline's instrumentalities to determine what could be contributing to what were thought to be false alarms. Unbeknownst to the crew during this period, and further complicating their efforts, however, was the fact that the pipeline's leak detection system was not functioning as designed, but was repeatedly and wrongly signaling a potential leak at the platform where no leak could be detected by the platform personnel and where no leak was occurring. Instead, as the factual record shows today, the leak occurred over four miles away, where the pipeline had been displaced more than 100 feet by a ship's anchor - a fact not shared with knowledge of that anchor -dragging incident. Had the crew known there was an actual oil spill in the water, they would have shut down the pipeline immediately. When a line ride the morning of October 2 identified a sheen in the water, the Company immediately began to execute its federally-approved oil spill response plan. BOEM Row/Segment Number P00547; Pipeline Segment #2610300

At approximately 18:50HRS; the M/V deckhand hooked the auxiliary line of the crane to a four-barrel drum rack (1,000 lbs.) that contained (4) empty DOT Drums and then provided a hoist hand signal to the crane operator. As the load was ascending, at approximately 1.5'- 4' FT off the back deck of the M/V, it contacted a tote tank and the securing binding chain of the tote tank. The binding chain and the sling assembly of a tote tank is where the initial load contact happened. As a result, the D-Style keeper pin inserted to secure the drum rack's door closed was damaged, failed, and the door opened. The drum rack's door then caught the interior railing of the M/V and (2) empty drums fell out of the drum rack. The crane operator and the boat captain conversed by radio and decided to continue with the lift, and the drum rack was offloaded and received on the platform. . The crane operator immediately reported the event to the Person-in-Charge (PIC) on the platform and then the Field Foreman and AOL's incident reporting requirements were initiated which included reporting the incident to the Field Foreman, Production Forman, and HSE Coordinator for investigation. Event Consequences 1. D-Style keeper pin was damaged resulting into failure. 2. Contents of the load became unsecured, and a portion fell to the deck of the M/V. 3. Barrel drum rack door hinge was damaged. There were no environmental impacts, or injuries to personnel because of this event.

description: At about 12:30hrs on 2/16/2023, an event on the Rig floor resulted in damage to the snub post used to secure the Rig floor hoists and to the cable on the 8 Ton hoist on the Main side Rig floor. As the TDS was lowered, the cable was inadvertently behind a pad eye on the Top drive that was positioned at 99' in the derrick and due to the offset between the cable snag and the snub post, the cable was tensioned enough to cause the snub post to break loose from the floor and be hoisted up with the cable as the cable twisted around itself. No Dropped objects occurred and no personnel were injured during this event. A thorough inspection of the TDS and the rigging at the crown was performed and no damage was observed. description: At approximately 18:20 hours on Monday, February 13, 2023, the ZZZ-9200 Power Generator shutdown. Mechanics responded to the generator enclosure and bypassed the enclosure's fire system in order to safely enter the enclosure. Mechanics inspected the engine's fuel filters, replaced the fuel filters, re-started the engine, and observed the engine run without a load for approximately 30 minutes. Approximately 5 minutes after loading the engine, the mechanics smelled and then saw smoke coming from the insulation on the left side turbocharger and associated air filter. When the insulation was removed, sparks and a small flame was observed. The fire was immediately extinguished with a handheld dry chemical fire extinguisher. The area was also soaked with firewater to ensure that the fire was completely extinguished. After disassembly and investigation to determine the cause of the fire, it was found that the air side of the left bank turbocharger had failed. The fins of the turbocharger made contact with the air side housing, causing sparks, which ignited the associated air filter. There were no injuries, no pollution, and only minor damage to equipment. The turbocharger and air filter were replaced at an estimated cost of $8,000. This facility was shut-in prior to and during this incident. Eymard" Generator Alternator Belt Failure - March 04, 2023, Incident Date Event Summary On March 04, 2023, at approximately 07:45 HRS, the Starboard Generator shut down. Upon the L/B Lacie G. Eymard Captains' arrival to the fiddley at the upper engine room, light smoke and a heavy burnt smell were observed. The captain immediately sounded the general alarm to muster all 3rd party personnel and informed the Vessel crew of the smoke and burnt smell. The Vessel's crew had readied and stretched the port side fire hose and closed the upper engine room door and engine room vents while the cook conducted roll call at the muster station. Before the captain opened the fiddley engine room door, he felt the door for heat with the back of his hand. No heat was felt, so the fiddley door was cautiously opened, and the starboard engine room was assessed. Smoke was observed from the generator alternator's belt. No flames were present, so the vents were opened back up, and the port generator was put online for the blowers to air out the engine room to change out the starboard generator's alternator. Captain deemed the area and situation to be safe and to resume work. Investigation Summary The investigation determined the following contributing factors: . Starboard Generator's Alternator bearing seized, locking up and cracking housing; this caused the drive belt to degrade, resulting in smoke accumulation within the engine room. . All 3rd party personnel aboard dawned Type 1 PFDs upon hearing the general alarm and congregated at the muster station. Non-essential personnel roll call was then completed. Captain arrived after clearing the engine room, proceeded with his crew's roll call, and explained the current problem and that it was resolved. Captain deemed the situation safe, and all clear was given. Normal duties resumed. Corrective Actions . The port generator was utilized to engage engine room blowers to ventilate the engine room. . The starboard generator alternator and belt were then replaced. Estimated costs: $175. Spare alternator/belts were available onboard and replaced following All Clear from Captain of Vessel by Captian/First Mate. **There were no injuries, fires, or environmental impacts due to this event.** -This is the Initial and Final Report-

description: INITIAL INVESTIGATION: Two large electrical transformers (3121 and 3122) were taken out of service and loaded into a 10'x30' basket (GJ016) utilizing the East Crane. The transformers were secured using rachet straps to keep the load from shifting during transport prior to the lift being executed. The lift was made from the Nakika on March 5th from the upper laydown area to the back of the Motor Vessel along with other miscellaneous items. The M/V finished operations on Nakika at approximately 18:00 and went to Ocean Blackhornet. While at the Ocean Blackhornet, basket GJ016 was lifted to be repositioned, more than 12 hours later from when it was backloaded at Nakika to make room for cargo to be loaded at the Ocean Blackhornet. When it was lifted, there was no residue on the deck. All the lifts were made at the Blackhornet and the Squall was headed back to C-Port. On the night of March 6th, the M/V backed into C-Port #3 to initiate the offloading process. At that time, the Captain informed C-Logistics Team that one of the electrical transformers were leaking transformer oil (Manufacturer DSI; Product Name: Beta Fluid; Product Description: Fire Resistant Transformer Oil) to the basket and to the back deck of the Squall. The M/V deck crew had not noticed anything until they went onto the deck to tie up the vessel upon arrival in the slip. The source was identified, electrical transformer tank reservoir through the damaged insulator (see pictures attached to this IRIS Report). Absorbent pads and other spill clean-up material was used to keep the transformer oil from spreading and potentially entering the GoM. Pictures and video footage have been obtained to try to get an understanding of when and how the insulator on the electrical transformer was damaged. It is unknown when it was damaged, but current evidence indicates that either the insulator was damaged by the 4-part wire rope sling or a load came into contact during the backload process by another load being set next to the electrical transformer basket. It is estimated, approximately 10 gallons of transformer oil leaked onto the deck of the boat and to the basket. description: While recovering the RST to deck with the crane, two attempts were made to land the RST out on deck on the test stump. On the first attempt, the load was not successfully landed out and the RST was placed back in the water. On the second attempt, the RST was landed against the work platform with integral capture frame to help control the load and land out the RST on the test stump. Contact between the RST and the capture frame resulted in superficial damage to the RST (Riserless Stimulation Tool) (a bent anode, a bent ROV grab bar, and a chaffed hose). The capture frame worked as designed and there were no injuries to personnel or contact between the load and other vessel structure. bp is currently in a stand down with crane personnel and crew as well as communicate with CI (C-Innovation). Updates: facility is Atlantis GC-787 -Why was the first attempt to land the RST not successful? The first attempt to land the RST was interrupted due to movement of the RST inside the maintenance frame, prior to landing out on the stump . The crane operator has decision rights on when to proceed with lifts and when to abort the lift. The RST was positioned inside the maintenance frame and final adjustments were being made to land it out, the crane operator did not like the movement he was seeing and decided to put it back in the water. Note: The water is considered our safe space. It was the only place we had to put it other than the stump. If we don't like the movement of the lift we simply put it back in the water. What were the weather conditions at the time of the incident? Wind: 8-12 kts SE - Current: 1.3 kts SW - Seas: 3-5ft. The weather really wasn't our issue, what we discovered is that we were having some abnormally long swell periods between 10 to 12 seconds. Normally, swell periods are much shorter. This allowed the RST to fully swing in a direction and build momentum. -Please attach all pictures of the damage? See Attached. -What is the estimated amount of damage associated with the incident. The anode was straightened and remains in use. The hose was replaced. Less than $500 value. The ROV grab handle was replaced. Less than $500 value. These items are kept in stock and considered consumable items due to wear and tear. -How long was BP in stand down mode with crane personnel? We suspended operations for 4 hours while the swell period shortened and allowed more favorable conditions to conduct the lift. We held approximate 15 minute safety stand downs with both crane crews following this incident. -What was found to be the cause of the incident? Description: At 05:30 hrs on 03/31/2023, our GC613A facility had a gas detector (GD-1702) that sounded the 10% LEL alarm (alarm only, no shut-in). At this time all personnel began mustering at their assigned location, with a full muster called at 05:35 hrs. The fire team was sent to investigate the gas alarm at 05:40 hrs. The team, once arriving in the area, determined that only gas detector (GD-1702) was alarming. The fire team then began to investigate the source of the gas. After a short investigation the team reported that the Cross Exchanger HBG-1525 was leaking oil and gas from the bottom of the unit. The Cross Exchanger HBG-1525 is over a solid containment deck and all fluid from the leak was contained and cleaned up after the all clear was given at 05:55 hrs. The facility was shut in by operations personnel. Our investigation into this incident shows that cooler than normal process liquids, caused hydrates in the system, which led to false readings in the level bridles for both the Inlet and IP Separators. This caused both separators to dump gas out of the liquid outlets (gas blow-by). This sent gas through the Cross Exchanger, cooling the plate's rubber gaskets. When the gaskets cooled, they expanded, and a leak developed. Currently the facility is shut-in awaiting repairs to be made to the Cross Exchanger. Path forward is to get a crew out to remove the plates and then send them in to be repaired. Once the plates have been repaired, we will have them sent back to the facility with a crew to have them re-installed. The estimated cost to repair the Cross Exchanger is $180,000.00. description: The Port Aft High Voltage Switch Board shut down on the rig. All persons were accounted for and no injuries were reported. The well work had been completed with the well in a state to hand over to production. The SSPT was aligned, the BOP had been recovered to the deck and we only had to recover a subsea basket and four of the ships transponders when the failure occurred. The vessel experienced a "Brown Out" just prior to 10 pm, 05/14/2023 of the Port side Transformer/Switchboard room, which shut down all of the engines on the Port Engine room and the ventilation to the space. All 6 thrusters were still available but at reduced power of 70 percent. There was no loss of station, the alarm was sounded and a full muster was performed. One of the Fire Teams was sent in the space to confirm that no fire was visible, however the space was full of dense smoke. No extinguishing agents were deployed during this event. The rig has been moved to shallow water for planned maintenance. Hess is offloading equipment and will be releasing the rig as it has completed it's scope of work.

description: Quarter North energy reports the following Crane Incident (Dropped Object) from GC65A; crew was removing a broken window air conditioning unit from the Emergency MCC building and lowering same with the crane from the E-Gen South Access/Landing area to a scrap metal basket. The A/C unit was rigged with 2 nylon straps side by side in a choker configuration around the outer housing. Once the lift was approximately 25 feet above the South access deck, the A/C unit slid out of the outer housing/casing and fell to the E-Gen South access deck below. The outer housing rigged with nylon straps was lowered by the crane to a safe location on the main deck. The dropped A/C unit weight approximately 100 pounds. No personnel were injured during this incident. A safety stand-down was called to discuss the incident and determine the causes. During the stand-down it was discovered that the employee performing rigging didn't recognize that the A/C unit was comprised of 2 separate pieces (the A/C unit & outer housing) and that the potential existed for the two sections to separate during lifting operations. Moving forward, PIC's will ensure that small items to be lifted are placed in a dedicated container / basket to be safely contained during transit. Update 6-1-23: Q:Which crane was in use at the time of the incident? A:The incident involved the South Crane. Q:Was a dropped object calculation completed? If so, please attach. A:Yes Attached Q:When the A/C unit slid out of the outer housing/casing and fell to the E-Gen South access deck, were there any nearby workers? A:There were no workers in the redzone. The only persons in proximity were 2 riggers stationed on each stairway leading to the landing where the AC unit fell. Q:What is QuarterNorth's policy on preventing personnel not involved in/unaware of crane operations within the redzone (lifting area)? A:SWP Section D, Chapter 3 6.2 Operating Practices:5. Loads shall not be moved over personnel. 6. All personnel must be clear of the load before it is lifted or moved Q:re these areas barricaded or isolated with red danger tape? For example, it is noted in one of the attached pictures that the A/C unit fell near a door. Were workers warned of an overhead lift outside that door by red danger tape inside possibly with a label stating why they should not exit? A:The door in the picture is access to the Emergency Generator Building. This building is only occupied for specific events such as maintenance, testing and/or if an upset event occurred that prompted the E-Gen to start up. At the time of the incident none of these specific events were ongoing, thus the building was unoccupied. Additionally, there is signage posted on the inside of this door which states "Danger - Crane in Use". (Picture attached). Additionally, during the lifting operation the stairs leading to the landing where the object fell was staged with rigging personnel to prevent others from accessing the redzone. Q:Were any additional safety measures in place at the time of the incident such as notifying workers not to enter the lifting area/redzone- such as in a Safety Meeting, over the Gai-tronics? A:The on tour crew participated in the pre-job meeting and JSA for the scope of work. As a common practice the team leads always mention in the morning, evening and Control of Work meetings when crane operations are to be performed, reminding all to be aware of the surroundings and to watch for crane activity. The crane operator also has a horn to warn anyone walking in or towards activities. This is indicated in section 4 and 6 in the JSA. (Attached) Q:Other than utilizing a dedicated container/basket moving forward, have any other safe work practices been identified that may be implemented to promote worker safety? A:In light of this incident we believe utilizing a dedicated cargo basket to transit small heavy objects is the best practice to prevent similar incidents. Additional coaching as to safe rigging practices was conducted by the team leads to ensure that the learnings from this event were passed on to the entire team. In line with continuous improvement, we are exploring additional safeguards to ensure that personnel are aware of and/or pre-warned prior to accessing any areas where overhead crane activity is active.

description: On 07/03/2023, at approximately 0840 hrs. while preparing to load casing from the M/V onto Olympus, as the crane operator began to cable up, noticed the aft sling sliding forward up the stand of drilling riser toward the center of the tubular and the tubular sliding through the wrap of the aft sling moving toward the stern of the M/V. The DSP was placed in the middle of the load to observe the lift and guide the crane from an advantage point that could see the entire task. Two extra deckhands were placed on either end to observe the lift and slings, and two deckhands were placed on the ends on tag lines on the opposite side to place pressure on the slings and keep them tight.

description: ***Final Report*** Incident Summary: Sometime between the hours of 1700 (07-24-2023) and 1100 hours (07-25-2023) the crane boom came into contact with the ISS owned gas buster vent line resulting in the vent line being bent. (Contact between the vent line and the bottom of the crane boom did not occur at the time damage was noticed). There were no injuries. Immediate Corrective Action: The UWA immediately called an all stop and had the crane operator inspect the crane boom while the ISS supervisor inspected the vent line. There was no apparent damage to the bottom of the crane boom, however there was an area where the paint had been scraped off. Paint on the vent line was cracked, however there did not appear to be any structural damage to either component. Investigation and Recurrence Prevention: The potential obstruction of the gas buster was identified in the JSA. The lift was not identified as a blind lift since the crane operator could see where the load started and was to be set down. It was identified during the investigation that during boom movement, there is a portion of the swing that the vent line was in a blind spot to the crane operator. Lifts planned for this boom path will be identified as a blind lift with a lift specific Lifting Operations Plan and lift specific JSA. These lifts may require placement of more than one Signalman in order to observe the entire load path; in these cases, both will be identified on the documentation. The Signalman is responsible for observing all aspects of the lift, including boom movement. Heightened awareness of this will be reviewed during the upcoming pre-tour SimOps / Safety Meetings. description: On Sept. 4th at approximately 09:00 hours an injury to an Contractor employee occurred after an unauthorized entry into a 10-foot diameter Heater Treater via a 24-inch manhole at HI 379-B. The Injured Person (IP) was attempting to use a 3-inch hose to vacuum fluids and sediment out of the tank through a vacuum pump and into a cuttings box. At some point in the operation the hose became vacuum locked onto a surface inside the tank. At this point, the IP without planning, risk assessing, direction, or authorization, initially placed approximately 60% of his body into the tank to free the hose end to break the suction hold and allow fluid to enter the hose. At some point, the worker completely entered the tank. His absence caused a co-worker, who was operating the vacuum pump within line of sight, to stop the job, look for the IP and call his supervisor for instructions and assistance when the IP could not be found.. Using a flashlight, the Contractor Job Superintendent saw the IP inside the tank laying under the fluid and initiated a rescue response. At this point of our investigation and analysis, it is apparent that Contractor personnel did not follow the restrictions and agreements made on the W&T Permit-to-Work that was issued on the day of the incident. In addition, they also did not follow their own JSEA and tank cleaning procedures. Lastly, the tank cleaner, who is a trained confined space entry supervisor as well as trained CSE rescuer also took it upon himself to enter the tank without planning, precautions, or authorization. In fact, there had been no planned tank entry, and the team specifically discussed not breaking the plane of the tank manway once it was opened to allow the vacuum hose to be used inside to vacuum the sediments from inside the tank. Immediate actions taken to prevent reoccurrence. A. description: ///This is the Initial and Final Report/// Event Description - Sequence / Timeline At approximately 06:30Hrs on 09/05/2020, personnel were being transferred from a motor vessel to EI-237K utilizing a Billy Pugh X-904 Rigid Personnel Transfer Basket from the stern designated area. The caught sling was identified, and the rigger was able to free the cable below the shackle attachment point rubber guard. The Personnel Basket was then lifted clear of the vessel and personnel, and then Stop-Work was initiated. Once the Personnel Basket had been inspected after freeing the cable, personnel aboard the vessel agreed to continue with the transfer. The JSA was annotated with the Stop-Work and approved to continue by UWA. Personnel completed the transfer from the motor vessel to the facility without further incident. Event Consequences . Off-axis hoisting of the X-904 Personnel Transfer Basket, resulting in a passenger jumping back onto the motor vessel. -There were no injuries or environmental impacts as a result of this event- ///This is the Initial and Final Report///

description: On 10/03/2023, between 6-8 am, Crane # 4 was recovering the ROV basket to surface. The ROV basket contained a hydraulic flying lead (HFL). When bringing the basket through the splash zone, it was observed that the HFL was hanging out of the basket. Upon sitting the basket on the deck, the HFL was still hanging over the handrail. Then, the HFL hose came free from within the basket and began going overboard until it was caught on some equipment. The Crane crew got the HFL hose secured and used the crane to hoist the HFL up in sections. Upon getting the hose back up on the deck, it was discovered to be damaged and not fit for duty. Pictures that were taken on the seafloor indicate that the HFL was secured in the basket and had no damage prior to being raised to the surface. It is believed that when the basket was hoisted through the splash zone, the wave action caused the hose to come partially out of basket and damaged during retrieval. It is estimated that a maximum of 6 gallons of Transaqua (hydraulic fluid within the HFL) was released to the water. According to the Manufacturer's Safety Data Sheet, Transaqua has a density of 1.071 g/cm3 and is composed of 40%-70% Ethylene Glycol (RQ of 5000 lbs.), 40%-70% water and 1%-5% Triethanolamine (RQ of 1000 lbs.). Based on this information, the event resulted in a chemical release to water below the reportable quantity threshold. The estimated amounts released are as follows: Estimated release of Ethylene Glycol ~ 21.452 lbs. - 37.541 lbs. Estimated release of Triethanolamine ~ 0.5363 lbs. - 2.6815 lbs. The weather and water conditions at time of incident: Sea state 1.2 @ 120, Swell 2 0.75 Wind was 16-19 knots. The replacement cost of the Hydraulic Flying Lead (HFL) was $120,500 USD.

description: At 4:30 am the facility lost power. PIC got up to restore power and noticed fire in gas generator housing and heard a popping noise. The platform ESD was activated shutting in the platform. The facility mechanic hit the emergency stop on the gas generator and the fire immediately went out on its own. The crew isolated the generator and secured the area. The back up, diesel fired generator was brought on-line to power the facility. No muster was required. Duty electrician is standing by on weather. Once clear the electrician will fly out to the facility to assist with the investigation. 29Nov23 Update: After further investigation The failure appears to have been caused by insulation failure one of the feed cable conductors. This caused a localized short circuit event, which then melted the neighboring conductors' insulation and the aluminum penetrating hub. The popping noise and fire, would be the melting of the aluminum, copper, and the insulation materials. Which ceased once the generator was shut down. Current condition: 1. Feeder cables have been removed from both the generator and breakers. 2. Damaged feeder cable has been temporarily terminated into the generator housing. Our remediation for this unit will be: 1. Replace the feed cable system from the gas generator to the main breaker. 2. Repair the damaged housing of the generator. 3. Repair the generator and voltage regulator that was damaged by the short circuit event. Estimated cost of repair 30,000.

description: . 0718 HC Gas level reach 40% LEL, Sound GA/PA and Muster personnel at the specific Safe Breathing Areas as per PIC. Fire pumps put online. Operations suspended and permits suspended. Heliport contacted to hold/divert Helicopters. Shaker House cleared of all personnel. Personnel inside the Accommodations mustered in the Mess Hall, while personnel working outside were instructed by the PIC to muster at their assigned lifeboat up forward. Wind was confirmed on the Portside, and Diverter confirmed to be set up for Starboard if needed. . 0719 Move Workboat standby . 0721 All PTWs suspended . 0722 Rapid Response Team on Standby . 0723 Well Secured, Mud Pump brought down . 0725 TOI and CVX Management Notified . 0732 Mud Pump back online . 0735 20% LEL at the two Shaker Exhaust Vents . 0743 30% LEL at the two Shaker Exhaust Vents / 3% at the Trip Tank . 0746 37% LEL at the two Shaker Exhaust Vents . 0747 Full Muster . 0748 40% LEL at Shaker Exhausts, 5% LEL at Trip Tank . 0756 60% LEL at Shaker Exhausts . 0800 10 minutes from Bottoms up, calculated . 0810 Bottoms up, 54% LEL at Shaker Exhaust Vents, 9% LEL at Trip Tank . 0817 HC Gas leveling off . 0907 Stand down from Emergency, continue to circulate Well free of gas at a controlled rate below GA/PA Alarm Limits. Leading up to the event, we were unable to stage the pumps back fast enough to keep the HC gas levels below hi-hi alarm threshold of 40% LEL at the shaker house exhaust vents, and the GA/PA was sounded to muster personnel per our Fire and Gas Philosophy. During the process, the Drill Crews shut in the Well and systematically staged the pumps up to circulate bottoms up to remove the HC Gas from the Riser and Well Bore. During the evolution, a maximum of 90% LEL was seen at the Shaker Exhaust Detector for a very short time when the gas peaked and just before it broke over. This was planned and expected as part of our process for removing gas as efficiently as possible. Once the gas levels dropped to below the alarm threshold and confirmed on a downward trend, the Command Team and CVX LDSR all agreed the Well was under full control and gas was indeed dropping to safe and manageable level so as to be able to secure from the event. Controls and parameters were confirmed, established, and put into place, and once it was safe to do so, we secured from the Muster and the PIC dismissed all personnel.

We will also be visiting with our compliance division for proper TSE location to share to make sure we are meeting regulation requirements on our rental equipment. The Subsea #2 crane safely recovered the THS to the rig with the crane. description: On December 26, 2023, at 0815, an operational incident occurred involving the MV during the offloading of cement sacks with the West Crane of the Platform. During this operation, the crane was engaged in lifting a 2000lb sack of cement mix when it became apparent that the sack had lost integrity, leading to the spillage of cement mix onto the deck. In consideration of the incoming helicopter, the crane operator opted to reposition the sack towards the bulwark of the boat to minimize the accumulation of cement mix on the deck. Once in a secure position, the crane operator locked the swing position of the crane boom and exited the crane cab. The Crane Operator elevated the sack to the Deck Supervisor, at which point there was only a minimal amount of mix remaining. The Deck Supervisor emptied the sack of the remaining mix and subsequently disposed of it. Approximately 1.5 hours after the incident, the Go Quest reported to EB-165A personnel a potential injury to the Deckhand related to the condition of the cement sack. The Deckhand claimed to have been struck by or caught between the cement bag and the bulwark. As a result, boat work was temporarily halted for further investigation. Further investigation is being conducted with this incident and all corrective actions are to be taken as necessary.

description: Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] Initial Immediate Notification and Subsequent Follow-up information on 3-13-2024. Following the event, an investigation was performed with participation by BSEE and USCG personnel. Following the initial Evidence Preservation Order, equipment associated with the event including breathing air compressors and the dive helmet were removed from the vessel and sent out for third party inspection for evaluation to determine whether there were any identified malfunctioning units or components that may have contributed to the issues experienced by the diver. All equipment and components inspected were verified to be properly functioning as intended during the inspection process. After exhausting potential equipment issues as causal factors in the event, all indications at this time point to the diver experiencing a non-work-related personal medication condition. To date, the autopsy report and associated toxicology report remain outstanding. This update is also being considered the Final Update and Submission for consideration as the final report.

description: Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] On 3/11/24 at approximately 11:15am, after receiving trash fluid from Mars MC807A, a TODO fitting failure occurred when disconnecting the hose. description: On 03/23/ 2024 at approximately 1630 hrs., at the Vito FPS (MC 939) technicians found heat damage to the outer covering of the ethernet cable to the boom tip camera on the east crane during maintenance work. Supervision was made aware of the finding and notification written to replace the cable. No known incident occurred near the time the damaged cable was discovered. However, the heat damage is believed to be from work performed months previously when moving material to north side of the facility. During the beginning of the activity heat detection alarms were activated on the crane boom when the boom was near an exhaust stack of a compressor. The camera was powered down on 2/12/24 for maintenance and then failed upon restoring power. There was no suspected cable damage at that time as this type of failure is not abnormal with these cameras. The work was immediately stopped, and the crane boom was moved to the cradle, an inspection was performed and there was no damage discovered at that time. All crane components remained fully functional, and the crane was put back into service. Minor damage to the outer covering on the following 3 electrical cables on the crane boom has been observed since the initial report. _x000D_ - Red boom obstruction light power cable (electrical power cable)_x000D_ - Aux load cell cable (electrical power cable)_x000D_ - Main load cell cable (electrical power cable)_x000D_ All three cables were disconnected for diagnostic testing, all tested good and have been reconnected. This additional damage is in the same area of the damaged ethernet cable. Please see attached photos of the damaged cable._x000D_ _x000D_ Updated 04/29/2024:_x000D_ What preventive measures will be taken to prevent the cables from exposure to heat from the compressor exhaust stack?_x000D_ Vito MC939 has reviewed the discovery of the damaged cables with all of the offshore personnel and also shared with onshore support. We have incorporated a step into the daily crane use JSA to cover potential heat exposure to crane boom and cables, and specifically call out that the crane boom cannot swing over compressor exhausts when the compressor units are in use and running._x000D_

description: On 5/3/24 at 2:49AM, the initial smoke detector YSH-5058 (2nd floor Laundry Room) came in alarm on the DCS. Fast response was dispatched, confirmed smoke, and alerted Control Room immediately. Control room activated muster alarm at 2:50AM and made verbal announcements to avoid the area and go to alternate muster stations. Fire team members found a dryer on fire and discharged 2.5 fire extinguishers into the dryer. The dryer was unplugged and then internals were sprayed with a fire hose to ensure no reflash. The fire lasted 5-7 minutes with the reflash from the time of the smoke. Once the fire was confirmed out with no additional reflashes at 3:01 AM, fire team began evacuating smoke and assessing surrounding areas above and below. No further damage was found and no damages to any other equipment. Full Muster was achieved at 3:09AM (19 min). All clear was given at 4:04AM and personnel were given command to stand down from the OIM, but to avoid the 2nd and 3rd floor main quarters. Fire team and support staff are currently working cleanup efforts and the investigation is ongoing to determine the root cause of the fire. No hot work was being performed and there were no injuries. Please see attached photos of the damaged dryer. The cost estimate to replace dryer is $1,800. _x000D_ _x000D_ Update 5/9/24: The fire was caused by soiled galley rags being dried in the dryer.

description: Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] 08.07.2024 [REDACTED_NAME] Q. Was the crane operator, operating despite the audible alarm sounding and the visual alarm? A. Based on the verified operation of the LSI. The operator would have been operating in the alarm status. But the LSI system will alarm at pre-set high angle @ 77 deg. And red indicator light. Q. Where are the set points for the alarms? A. Audible Alarm Set - 77 degrees or 47.3 Radius Feet A. Visual Alarm Set - @ 65 degrees a single beep with yellow caution symbol to indicate boom slow down angle has been reached. Then @ 77 degrees the LSI gives an indication RED symbol light with a constant audible Alarm. Q. What is the model number on for the LSI? A. GS820 / ID.# 82010 Q. What date was the LSI install? A. It was installed by shell before ENVEN purchased of GC158 / owner of GC158 Now Talos Energy The design of the Boom Angle Indicator is very complex, and LSI does not share the intricate design of the components. The way it was explained to me, "it is mounted to the boom centerline and has an internal component, designed like a pendulum that references center of gravity with a pivot point that is fixed to calculate the angle". This would explain, if there is an abrupt start or stop, this "pendulum" would be susceptible to the inertia imposed by either motion causing the Boom Angle reading to fluctuate. 07.31.2024 [REDACTED_NAME] Q. Talos exhibited evidence that verified that the crane's HAKO device was not bypassed at the time of the incident. Please provide all documents associated with the two-key system that prevents the bypass of safety devices on the crane such as the bypass of the HAKO without administrative approval. A. Talos had a crane specialist ([REDACTED_NAME]) with Seatrax conduct a thorough review of the American Aero Crane hydraulic system at GC 158 Brutus facility. His findings of the hydraulic system for the crane determines the key switch is NOT an override for the HAKO. When crane is boomed up and trips the HAKO the key switch will not override the HAKO function. His review of the hydraulic system also verified there is no valve between the boom lever and the HAKO device. Therefore, there is no way to bypass or override the HAKO. The key switch is set up to override the Anti Two Blocking system for the main and aux lines. If for some reason the main or aux line is raised high enough to trip the Anti Two Block on either line, it will take two personnel to override the Anti Two Block system. One individual will have to be in the crane cab to function the lever to lower the line and the other person will need to be at the key switch holding the key rotated to bypass the Antil Two Block to override the tripped device. B. Let me try to clarify this HAKO function on the American Aero cranes at GC158 Brutus. The key switch is not an override for the boom up function, rather it is an override for the anti-two block system which are two separate safety systems. When the boom comes up high enough to trip the HAKO, the key switch will not override that HAKO function. If someone inserts the key and holds it on (spring loaded switch), the boom winch still will not operate to come up any higher. The purpose of the key switch is only to override the anti-two block system to allow function of the aux or main hoist if the anti-two block is malfunctioning to allow the operator to be able to set the load down and boom down so the anti-two block system can be repaired. In normal operation, when the aux or main hoist is hoisted up too far and trips the anti-two block device, it stops the aux or main hoist from hoisting up any further to prevent pulling the main block or overhaul ball up to the sheaves in the boom tip. The operator can then hoist down to get it out of alarm. Q. Please attach all logs retained, written procedures, as well as an explanation of how the system works. A. description: Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] This is a 6 hr report to eWell in lieu of Immediate Reporting. At 16:40 on the Diamond Black Lion, a dropped wellbore clean out assembly fell across the derrick and came to rest on the STBD FWD derrick beam by MW maintenance basket. While POOH on main well center, the aux well AD was in the process of moving a 4-1/2" Halliburton WBCO assembly using the aux well hydraracker from row 23 to row 24 in the derrick. Employee positioned the main head to low on the assembly, so it could set the stand back into the finger board, closed the fingers and sat assembly down in setback. When the employee opened his main head and retracted it, the top finger latch was closed, and the bottom finger was still up. The assembly then started to bow causing the upper portion of the assembly to come out of the upper board finger latch. Assembly then fell across the derrick and came to rest on the STBD FWD derrick beam by MW maintenance basket. What were the corrective actions taken for future operations? . Update ALL SSP's that reference use of the hydraracker for either racking back pipe or removing pipe from the derrick to highlight designating one flagger on the main level of the rig floor inside of the red zone to watch the lower fingerboard pending the person on the top level is unable to have a bird's eye view of the fingers. Also, make sure we add a note that the flagger could have multiple tasks during this time i.e. watching the lower fingerboard and flagging the hydraracker operator for gripper placement on the pipe. . Create a ticket and reach out to NOV to inquire if any changes can be made to their system for finger failure. When commanding finger latch closed, if the upper finger latch closes but the lower finger latch doesn't, the SDI screen will still show all fingers are closed. Therefore, we have to manually send personnel in the line of fire to confirm if the fingers are up or down. Attached all documentation provided to close the CAPA. Including emails and open/close ticket item. . Formulate a plan to purchase and install Drill Collar finger latches from American Block. Update the progress journal once they are received on board and safely installed. . Update all SSP's regarding handling BHA and racking it back in the derrick or retrieving it from the derrick. The SSP's needs to highlight that anytime we are picking up BHA and racking it back, make sure we update the BHA tally with the correct MAE position height and if any function will require the operator to utilize the override button. Also, when retrieving the BHA from the setback area, make sure we reference the BHA tally prior to removing the assembly. . Create a thorough and detailed personnel training program for all SSE's and mentors. Established a sound foundation that will help personnel become comfortable when facing adversity while also being decisive and consistent with their decision making. Generate a system that will be managed correctly and user friendly. . Have all Drill Crews review the updated SSP's regarding having a designated flagger inside of the red zone on the main level to watch the lower fingerboard and/or flag the hydraracker operator for head placement on a tool racked back in the derrick. Close this CAPA by attaching a signoff sheet with the signatures from all Drill Crew members acknowledging receipt of the changes made.

description: Contractor Company: Champagne Energy and Environmental Solutions Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] While contractors working for Transco, performing decommissioning work on PSN 5136, in the SP-10 block of the gulf of mexico on July 20th, 2024, the following incident occurred: When attempting to lift up jet pump and move it to the MV Port Eads, the LB Joni's JP-33 rigging hardware got hung up on, and damaged the air manifold and frame jet pump of the unit. The air manifold was damaged by the interaction with the rigging hardware and the frame was damaged due to its subsequent impact with the back of the vessel. The damage was minor and estimated to be around $1000 to repair. There were no injuries or crane damage associated with the incident. description: Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] On August 20, 2024 at approximately 04:30, the crane crew was making a lift of a 4x4x4 basket from the accumulator deck to the plus 50 deck below. The DSP advised the crane operator to come up on the basket. The basket was empty and located three inches to the side of the windwall and the lip of the basket was three inches different in height than the railing of the windwall. The crane operator said that the weight was good so he began to make the lift. As soon as the crane operator began to make the lift, the basket made contact with and was hung beneath the railing of the windwall. The DSP who was ten foot back and at a safe distance, told the crane operator, all stop, over the radio. Before the crane operator had stopped the lift, one leg of the four part sling had broken. The DSP again was at a safe distance away from the load. After further inspection by the crane mechanic it was also found that the crane hook had minor stretch to the opening of the hook rendering it out of service. The damaged items were replaced before putting the crane back in service. It should be noted that the basket was only lifted 3 inches off the deck when it hung up on the structure. There were no injuries reported. Cost of sling was under $500 and The crane hook assembly was about $19,000. Please see attached photos, permit, JSA and certificates. Corrective Actions: The damaged items were replaced before putting the crane back in service. A meeting was held with crane crews to speak about using a longer sling so as to keep the crane hook away from the Windwall. This will help prevent the lift from getting hung up. Disseminate the learning to all 4 of crews as lessons learned. Update 9/6/24: QUESTION: According to Shell's Critical Lift Plan, it was checked off to have extra riggers. How many riggers were used to control the critical lift? ANSWER: Extra riggers are only added as needed per Lifting plan. See attached section of lifting plan that highlights the text. It was not needed here and therefore we had two. Adding extra riggers in this tight area would have increased the risk. QUESTION: How did the riggers attempt to control the lift? extra tag lines? push/pull poles? hands-on load? ANSWER: The riggers attempted to control the lift with tag lines. QUESTION: What actions could have prevented this incident. ANSWER: Due to the tight area there will be no longer allowed to use baskets in this area. description: On 9/20/24 at approximately 10:45AM, while preparing for the ISIP inspection and setting up the ventilation equipment, a ventilation fan was taken out of the aluminum storage cabinet. After the incident, fluid residue was found inside the fan plug housing, which was not visible beforehand and was only noticed due to the hole caused by the arcing. description: RUE: OCS-G30372_x000D_ Description: _x000D_ On Tuesday, September 24, 2024, at approximately 1010hrs, a Murphy Crane Operator was offloading and backloading the boat. Meanwhile, the Crane Operator raised the stinger roughly 20 feet, boomed up, and began swinging towards the West Laydown Area. Misjudging the amount of clearance, the stinger caught the middle rail on the Living Quarters roof NW handrail._x000D_ Immediate Actions: _x000D_ The Crane Operator reported the incident to the OIM and Head Operator. The operators then installed a hard barricade and danger tape to prevent access to the area._x000D_ No injuries or pollution. Damage cost range between $1,725-$3,625. _x000D_ Corrective Actions:_x000D_ 1) Hard Barricaded Area and Red Danger Taped across barricade (as above)_x000D_ 2) Reiterated and made sure everyone understood that no one is rushing anyone for any job. Ensure you have cabled up higher than everything surrounding your lifting area and then proceed to swing and position over the next lift._x000D_ 2) Be aware of surroundings at all times. _x000D_ 3) If you aren't completely sure you are clear, stop the job and call additional help (a spotter) to go to area in question and ask them to signal you. description: Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] On 10/24/2024 at 0222 hrs., While rigging down the wireline sheave from the CTLF, IP secured the tugger line to the wireline sheave and signaled the tugger operator to cable up. During this process, the top counterweight contacted a pad eye on the CTFL, causing it to become temporarily lodged. Before IP could signal the tugger operator to stop, the counterweight dislodged. This resulted in the wireline sheave striking the IP in the lower back. IP was lowered down to the rig floor and was taken to medic for further evaluation. After consultation with onshore medical team, IP was sent ashore for further evaluation. IP was flown in via Medivac Helo at 0829 hrs. on 10/24/2024. Please see attached JSA, operation procedures, man rider training, photos, pre-tour review roster, witness statements and incident report. Corrective Actions: Held stand down with crews to discuss incident, line of fire and establish further controls, corrective actions, surroundings awareness, & communications, in addition to further risks management techniques. Update 11/4/24: IP started days off on 10/25/24. IP had a CT scan and X-rays done with results both negative and to date the IP has not been given any restrictions. On site prescription medication was the only thing prescribed. IP is expected back for the next hitch. Update: 12/12/2024: Due to pain level of the IP, the IP has not been released, and a follow up appointment is currently being scheduled. We have not been able to obtain any documentation at this time. Updated: 1/22/25 Please see attached medical note.

description: Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] This evening while conducting lifting activities on the Mid Deck Production, a connex contacted an isolation valve downstream of the clay valve for Zone 12 of the firewater deluge system. Date: 11/1/24 Time: ~8:30PM Summary: Starboard forward crane was attempting to set a connex in place. Deck crew observed there was not enough room so lift was swung out of the way and grating was shifted over with a pallet jack to provide additional deck space. Lift was swung back over landing area, but it was still slightly over the grating. Tag lines and push poles were utilized to move the lift over due to crane boom limitations. Platform motion occurred while tag lines and push poles were being used and the load contacted the valve handle. Deck crew notified Crane Operator and Topside Deck Operator who further escalated notifications. Assessment of the valve is that it is still functional and no damage is seen on the fiber bond piping. Before returning to work we took a pause to understand what happened with the Crane Crew and Deck Operator. We reiterated there was no need to have perceived pressure about the lifting activities. Then we notified the BP and Valaris OIMs before allowing the crane crew to go back to work. Attached are photos. Initial Actions Taken: The Deck crew notified Crane Operator and Topside Deck Operator who further escalated notifications. OIM and WSL notified. Assessed condition of the valve and determined that it is still functional, and no damage is seen on the fiber bond piping. Held safety stand down with crew to discuss incident and controls to prevent reoccurrence. Corrective Actions: OIM to discuss incident in next 4X Weekly safety meeting reinforcing expectations to ensure landing zones have sufficient space before landing loads, and taking the time needed to clear out landing zones. DF to remove extra grating from landing zone to provide additional space for landing connex. DF to ensure landing zone remains clear before going forward. If landing zone doesn't have sufficient space, remove extra material or equipment before landing loads in that area.

description: Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] On 10/25/2024 at 1000hrs., worker noticed synthetic base mud (SBM) overflowing from the end of auger system. The bottom shaker motor had kicked off causing the mud to flow over the shaker instead of through it. The SBM flowed into the auger causing it to overflow at the end of the auger. description: On 11/16/2024 at 0849 hrs., an employee walking by a battery room on deck, observed through the door window and saw smoke in battery room. Immediate notification to the control room via gaitronics was made, which initiated ESD/Blowdown and full muster of personnel. Electrical Power was then isolated to that room. Emergency response was activated and determined that a cell short causing overheating and melting of the battery case to be the culprit. The room was opened and cleared of smoke. Authorized electrical personnel then entered donning appropriate PPE and disconnected the compromised battery and placed it in overpack for disposal. _x000D_ The event occurred in AECC Battery Room northeast deck #3. There was NO visible flame, just smoke and smoldering. Report was made to the control from at 0849 hrs. and power secured at 0902 hrs. When it was deemed safe, the battery was removed from the series at 0934 hrs. There was one 2.5 volt battery damaged. There were no injuries related to the incident. Estimate damage repair cost is less than $1000. No hot work was taking place. Please see attached photos._x000D_ _x000D_ Corrective Actions:_x000D_ This event was not associated with any work activity. The battery room is currently out of service. The purpose of this battery room is to provide DC backup power to the Post Lube Oil Pump for FGC#1. FGC #1 is also out of service._x000D_ _x000D_ Updated 12/4/24:_x000D_ QUESTION: Has it been determined how long the compromised battery had been in service?_x000D_ ANSWER: The batteries were manufactured and installed in 2010 and are good for 20 years. description: Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] Please provide the identification of the glycol contactor Glycol Contactor Identification: MAF-0234 Acadian Contractor supervisor saw a flame coming from dehydration after scrubber MBF-0233. There was a loud pop and flame flare out then went away. Immediately made sure no hot work was being conducted on anything related. Shut down all jobs. Reported to supervisor then went back to area with a gas detector to be sure area was safe to investigate cause of incident. 2024-12-02 - - In response to fire incident on GC-52-CPP on Nov 20, 2024. On November 20,2024 an incident occurred on GC-52-CPP during cleanout operations being performed by Acadian Contractors cleaning crew on the Dehy Afterscrubber MBF-0233. Cleaning crew were on deck but not in immediate area, a loud noise was noticed, upon investigating the noise it was noticed that a flame came from the vessel, crew evacuated the area and notified facility PIC. There was no Hot Work being performed on GC-52-CPP at the time of the incident, there was no Injuries to crew, and no damage to equipment. The Platform had been shut in since Aprill 2024 for decommissioning activities and all vessels had been previously flushed, filled and drained utilizing seawater to reduce the amount of hydrocarbons in the vessels for cleanout. An onsite investigation conducted with BSEE and Operations personnel, along with interviews of all personnel involved, concluded there was no definitive proof of source of ignition, two possible sources of ignition were identified as .Static Charge due to the dry air conditions and cooler weather. . Possible Pyrophoric scale as explained in BSEE Safety Alert No. 462, May 12, 2023. Although filling and flushing operations were conducted with seawater, the vessel was never isolated from nearby vessels with the use of blind flanges or spectacles, nor purged of hydrocarbon gas utilizing an inert gas like nitrogen. The manhole cover was opened facing the wind allowing air to enter the vessel and did not allow a true reading on the gas monitor. Since the incident MCOP has implemented the following .All vessels are to be isolated from all other vessels during the cleaning process . All vessels should be purged utilizing an inert gas prior to cleaning operations.

description: Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] On 12/02/24 at approximately 1000 hours, while OSV [REDACTED_NAME] was offloading cargo to [REDACTED_NAME], a 90ft basket swung and broke the water tight call box on the aft deck phone.
