No other injuries or damages were noted and or reported. Please see attached [REDACTED_MEDICAL_DETAIL], witness statement, weather report, and photos. Learnings: Elevated sea state combined with long lifts was the root cause of the incident. When lifting long baskets there is a chance the ends will get inside the headache rack. With the vessel rolling and the wind blowing on the basket, it's not always possible for the crane operator to keep the lift laying alongside the headache rack. When loading the vessel, the long baskets are accounted for and try to keep the ends from more critical sections ex mud, dry bulk and fuel piping and venting. With the elevated sea state, it's safer to keep the crew clear from the basket preventing injuries. As soon as practical, a documented safety meeting with all crewmembers will be held to share this scenario and the prevented measures above. The corrective action from the rig's standpoint to prevent a similar situation in the future would be for the vessel to not mount such equipment on the bumper railing subject to and in proximity of lifts.

Each proppant bag consists of four sides, weighs approximately 1.75 metric tons, and measures approximately 38 inches high by 35 inches wide. A fourth bag is between every two vertical rows to try and prevent the bags from falling. The fourth bag does not interlock with the next column of bags; it simply sits between two vertical rows of bags. The method used to remove the stacked proppant bags consist of one worker standing on the forklift tines while being lifted approximately 9 feet in the air then climbing onto the proppant bags, without fall protection. He stands on the proppant bags and leans over to the next bag to lift the bag straps enabling the forklift operator to insert the tines between the straps. The forklift operator removes the bag from the stack and places it next to the loading dock. This procedure is repeated until the final bag is on the ground. Employee #1 who was picking up the bag straps, finished spotting for one of the forklift operators and was standing on the ground approximately 6 feet from a row of stacked bags. description: At 11:30 a.m. on February 1, 2019, an employee was working for a firm that made custom signs, such as menu boards, real estate signs, fascia, and lighting accent bands. There were no employees at the worksite at the time of inspection. The last day employees worked per the employer was February 15, 2019. The manufacturing involved the use of metalworking machinery and woodworking machinery. This included but not limited to punch presses, press brakes, table saws, and chop saws. The bracket was made of steel and approximately 3.175 millimeters (0.125 inches) thick. The holes were approximately 9.525 millimeters (0.375 inches) in diameter. The design called for one hole on each side of the L-bracket. The punch die was a single operation C-frame die, which was secured to the bolster plate on the bed of the punch press. The die had feed clearance for the 3.175-millimeter (0.125-inch) thick bracket. The punch tip was in an enclosed throat. In practice, the employee would place the bracket into the feed slot in the die and engage the foot pedal to operate the press. The employee would then manually turn the bracket 45 degrees, and the second side would be punched. On the day of the incident, the employee had not completed setting up of the press opening or cycle setting before he engaged the foot pedal as he adjusted the placement of the bracket in the die. The employee was transported to UCI medical center for treatment. He was not hospitalized. Following a later request by the Division, the hospital did not find any mediical records for the employee. description: At approximately 6:20 a.m. on Wednesday, August 5, 2020, an employee was working for an intermodal freight transport company or trucking carrier. He picked up and drove semi-trailer truck number P9032 into the firm's yard. He located shipping container number BMOU3075767. He backed his truck into the chassis and secured it to the fifth wheel mechanism, located at the rear of the truck. He stepped out of the truck cabin to attach the red and blue air lines to the chassis along with the electric cable. Once these were securely connected, the employee walked around the truck to get access to the crank of the landing gear legs. Either he did not apply the brakes, or the brakes were ineffective. As the landing gear legs retracted up off the ground, the truck and chassis rolled backward and sideways toward the employee. The employee was caught in between the moving chassis container and another stationary container located behind him. He was ultimately pinned between these two containers. A coworker, who was working nearby, discovered the employee pinned between the two containers and immediately entered the cabin of truck number P9032. The coworker applied both the trailer air supply brakes and the parking brakes. The employee was crushed between two shipping containers and was killed. The coworker said he grabbed his handkerchief and started applying pressure but noticed that employee was not responding. He called for EMS and they arrived in about 20 to 30 minutes. description: Due to the pipeline pump not speeding up since 01.24.2021, the operator began to troubleshoot pipeline pump #1 and found that the wire had cracked and brunt the terminal connector on the power box. 02.23.2021: Investigative findings: - The power leads for the junction block terminate inside of protective housing. - The power leads are secured by tightening machine screws set into the terminal block. - Over time, the machine screws appear to have loosened causing an incomplete (loose) connection inside the terminal block. The loose connection resulted in line resistance. - As the current was passed through the connection, an arc was generated. Root Cause: - Upon investigation, it was determined that the plausible fault for the incident was due to vibration caused by Pipeline Pump #1. The vibration caused the machine screws used to secure the wire leads into the terminal block to back out. The result of the loosened connections was resistance (across the connection). The increase in resistance (>0 ohms) caused the connection to heat up and the resulting arc.

While the load was held in position the M/V began to reverse toward the platform and under the load. . Once in position to receive the load the M/V was exposed to side sea conditions which swayed the vessel up during side-to-side (transverse axis) movements. . At that time, the bottom of the tote tank encountered one of the handrails of a gangway. . As the boat leveled to its original elevation, the crane operator lifted the load slightly then swung the tote tank to the left, away from the gangway and then lowered the tote tank to the deck of the M/V. . Once backloading operations were complete the crane operator reported the event to the Person-in-Charge (PIC) on the platform and then the Field Foreman and AOL's incident reporting requirements were initiated which included reporting the incident to the Field Foreman, Production Forman, and HSE Coordinator for investigation. Event Consequences 1. Gangway handrail was bent downward, and a weld was broken on the base of a socket which connects the handrail to the walking plank. description: What Happened? At approximately 08:22 on April 2nd while operating in a Split-Bus configuration (i.e., 3 independent, high voltage switchboards), the Starboard high voltage switchboard experienced a partial blackout due to low voltage from the online Diesel Generator (DG) #2. An automatic "All-Start" command was initiated due to loss of voltage. Subsequently, DG #1 started but failed to connect to the starboard bus, due to a sync failure caused by the voltage deviation caused by DG #2. As a result of the starboard engine room blackout, thrusters T2 and T4 dropped offline, and there was a loss of power to several critical drill floor systems (including the topdrive and drawworks). The rig was able to maintain station with four (4) thrusters with no issue. Initial troubleshooting discovered a failed Phase Monitoring Relay inhibited the ability to close the ship's service transformer that supplies power to the auxiliaries. Continued inspection identified that DG #2 had a break in one of the windings on the exciter (i.e., armature winding). Once DG#2 was taken offline, DG #1 was restarted and placed online powering the starboard bus with no issue. Event Timeline 20:22 DG #2 voltage alarm 20:23 DG #2 Automatic Voltage Regulator (AVR) alarm 20:24 DG #1 Sync Failure but running offline (Other two Switchboards had both engines running after "All-Start") 20:31 DG #1 Connected 20:41 DG #2 Shutdown 01:00 Check control system and change out Phase Monitoring Relay for Pre Mag-Distribution panel. 03:00 Failed Relay replaced; reset drilling equipment and bring T2 & T4 back online (Starboard bus). Perform Isolations in order to continue troubleshooting & diagnostics of DG #2 generator (windings / diodes / rectifiers). Early Learnings: Subsequent Findings and Actions: . The break in the winding appears to have initiated the failure of DG #2 to supply the designed output voltage and subsequent internal arcing resulted in voltage spikes that led to the failure of the Phase Monitoring Relay. This failed relay and the voltage imbalance from DG #2 inhibited the ability to close the ship service transformer and prevented DG #1 from syncing after "All-Start". . DG #2 is temporarily out of commission, until the exciter is replaced, or rebuilt. The rig will remain in a Split- (Open) Bus configuration. An operational hazard assessment will be required prior to going to a 2+1 bus configuration for any for any Split-Bus deviation request, outside those necessitated by the Well Specific Operating Criteria (WSOC). A Common-(Closed) Bus arrangement is not recommended under any circumstances.

description: 04.02.23 Initial Incident Description: Current site activity is pipeline flushing operations. At about 12.20 pm, the platform crane operator had successfully lower (food lunches) via personnel basket to the MV. A contractor pump tech. aboard the vessel retrieved the food-lunch package from the basket. As the crane operator began hoisting the personnel basket apparently the pump tech. inadvertently was standing or stepped on the basket's tag line as it moved upward causing him to fall on the deck (surface level to surface level) landing on his left shoulder. Operations were stopped to assist the falling worker. The injured person (IP) states he has discomfort in his left-shoulder. Air transportation was secured for pick-up and transfer. The IP's employer met him and transported him to the hospital seeking further medical evaluation and/or treatment. An investigation of this incident as been initiated and should conclude by April 21st, 2023. 04.14.2023 update: Injured worker has been diagnosed with a left (L) labrum tear and has not returned to work. He is participating in physical therapy and will be medically re-evaluated on May 2nd. WhiteFleet Operating is meeting with contractors involved to complete the incident investigation, determine contributing cause(s) and identify action(s) to prevent a recurrence. Final Update: The managements of WhiteFleet Operating LLC and Crane Contractor have met to discuss the incident, identify lessons learned and develop preventive actions. Contributing cause(s) identified from the investigation were: (1) Injured Person (Pump Tech.) post removing the material package (lunch box) from the personnel basket turned away to leave without providing a designated signal to the Crane Operator to hoist; nor did he see the tag line he tended previously to land the basket beneath his foot upon his first steps; (2) Crane Operator hoisted the personnel basket pre-maturely without a designated signal from the (Pump Tech.) he did not visually confirm clearance of the basket and/or intention of tending the tag line prior to hoisting by the Pump Tech; (3) the Crane Operator failed to call "Stop Work" to ensure the rigger tender the basket tag line as he did before. Preventive Actions: Whitefleet Operating & Contractor managements have communicated the incident findings and following preventive actions to fleet operations in effort to heighten procedural & situational awareness when landing and hoisting the personnel basket whether on facility deck and/or on a vessel. Personnel basket lifts will require effective communication between Crane Operator and designated tenders (hand signal and/or verbal); WhiteFleet Operating will develop and communicate a Safety Alert of this event and its learnings for awareness purposes throughout fleet operations to prevent a future re-occurrence.

description: At approximately 06:10am, while conducting planned over boarding operations of Frac Fluid the team diverted to begin catching fluid in the Concentric Tank and closed the valve to stop the overboard process. There was a marked reduction in flow rate. Approximately 15 minutes after closing the valve there was still a noticeable amount of fluid bleeding through valve into the overboard line. The Pumphand was instructed to close the overboard and utilized an alternate line-up (Reverse Out Line) that did not tie into the overboard valve. Over the 15 minutes it was estimated 5 bbls of Zinc Bromide Fluid lost overboard. This is suspected to have occurred due to a washed out three-way manual valve. Currently alternate line is being used until the valve can be changed out. The National Response Center (NRC) was notified at 9:26 AM report # 1368099. Please see attached, Safety Data sheet, and photos showing the valve location and pathway to the overboard line. Sea and wind conditions during the time of the incident: Seas & Swell - Calm, 0 ft. K - Current: 1.8kt from 062 degrees Surface Current: 0.5kt toward 334 degrees Barometer - 1011.3 Clouds - 3/8 Visibility - 12 nm Air - 25.7 degrees C Sea - 26 degrees C Pitch - 0 degrees Roll - 0 degrees Heave - 0.0 ft Update per email sent 6/20/23: Upon further investigation and confirmation with our environmental engineers, it has been determined that the volume lost overboard on 5-24-2023 was overestimated during the original notification. Once the job was completed and the final straps of fluid was tallied, all fluid was accounted for in the mud pits and 3 bbls was missing from the concentric tank which is where gel fluid was being diverted. The original report did not include the density of the fluid which was determined to be 15.0 ppg CaBr2/ZnBr mix. With this new information, it has been determined that no regulatory agency reporting was actually necessary but could not be confirmed within the 6-hour verbal reporting window. The requirement for reporting a discharge of the fluid that was in use at the time has a reportable quantity (RQ) of 1000 lbs. per the attached SDS and page 89 of List of Lists: https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2022-12/List_of_Lists_Compiled_December%202022.pdf 15.0ppg fluid mix will equal 71lbs per bbls per Tetra's mix chart. 3bbls lost = 213.9lbs or 5bbls lost = 356.5lbs are both non-reportable quantities. description: At approximately 9:20 am on 6/21/23, Perdido experienced a Platform shut down due to a VFD failure. The "variable frequency device" is the controller for the caisson ESPs located in the platform's subsea MMC control room. The smoke detectors in the subsea control building were automatically activated by the smoke that was released from the VFD cabinet. This initiated a PSD - Platform Shut Down. A full muster was accounted for in 7 minutes. No escalation outside of the subsea MMC control room. The ICS team dispatched the fire team to a staging area and then to the Sub-Sea MCC. The fire team only observed smoke (no fire) from the VFD failure. Once the area was secured, an electrician was then dispatched to the building to begin surveying the cabinets. No notable temperature differences noted on the outside of the cabinets. Permission was given to open the cabinet on A and a temperature in excess of 350F was observed. Continued survey of the B, C, and D cabinets and ~210F temperature was observed. At that point, the team felt they had identified and isolated the source of the smoke which was detected. A fire watch was staged and the fire team to report back to debunker. The community was allowed to leave muster but not allowed to return to work. Recovery: The building was ventilated, smoke cleared, and AHU's returned to service. Once all smoke detectors were clear, the doors were closed to the building and smoke detection was continuously monitored. A LOTO was installed on the electrical breakers for ESP-A VFD. The team then proceeded to apply power to the other available ESP VFD's in the building to verify their health (B, C, D). All appeared to have no issues. General community was then allowed to return to work. After speaking with Marco DeLeon w/BSEE and getting a verbal approval to start, the crew proceeded to run ESP - B to secure part of the sub-sea system for flow assurance (hydrate prevention). The team then moved on to ESP-D followed by ESP-C, ensuring their health. Once B-caisson wells were deemed safe they were started on initial ramps. After all three ESP's were verified healthy, BSEE was notified through the afterhours hotline with an update. Costs: As far as repair costs, the crew is in the process of changing out the entire cabinet and start over with fresh equipment. The cost of the new cabinet is approximately $65,000 with one currently on location. The Perdido leadership team feels that this will be the safest and most efficient way to ensure safe production from ESP "A". Go forward plan: -Trouble shoot ESP-A VFD to identify failure -Change the reactor cabinet and output switch section of VFD -Commission and return to service Production Impact: Production loss estimated after failure -15,789 BOPD, 12083 GAS = -17803BEQ Power: ESP VFD's voltage rating is 6.9KV Update: 7/18/23: RCFA report attached.

description: A small flame was witnessed by two personnel on the turbo insulation blanket of compressor at our SM 99A facility. The flame was quickly extinguished by one personnel using a nearby water hose. It should be noted that the water hose used was utility water and not part of the fire water system. Although no damage was identified by the flame, the initial investigation revealed that a bracket, which helps support the expansion joint for the turbo, had broken. The resulting vibration caused the expansion joint to crack, and once it cracked, the hot exhaust contacted the exhaust's blanket. This led to oily/coolant residue on the exhaust's blanket to flame. There were no injuries resulting from this incident and current POB at the facility is 9. The facility remains on-line however, the compressor was shut-in and will remain shut-in until repairs are made. Initial first report was made to BSEE Lafayette afterhours line. Update 6/29: Upon further investigation, it has been determined that the exhaust's expansion joint does not have a crack. However, oil residue was found on the blanket, and it was determined that the heat from the exhaust caused this residue to ignite. Extensive maintenance was conducted on the compressor prior to the incident, which involved replacing the turbo. It is believed that either oil from the replaced turbo or coolant during maintenance became the source of the residue on the exhaust's blanket. As a result, both the expansion joint and the exhaust blanket have been replaced. We are confident that we have successfully eliminated the cause of this incident.

description: This is the Initial and Final Report Investigation Summary/Event Description: On November 09, 2023, at 09:00HRS an alarm was automatically sounded, and the platform shut because of an activated Temperature Safety Element (TSE). All platform personnel immediately responded and convened at the muster station. All personnel were accounted for within a few minutes of the alarm. Production operating personnel then proceeded to the Master Panel of the platform to investigate which TSE Zone could be identified indicating TSE pressure was lost. Production operators determined that the activation was within Zone No. 3 therefore began inspecting all the permanent positioned TSEs equipped for the Float Cell and the generators. After inspecting Zone No. 3 without an activation discovery within the TSE loops, Production Operators moved to inspect the temporary TSE loops that support construction rental equipment, e.g., air compressors and welding machines. It was then that the temporary TSE loop on a welding machine was immediately noticed as having a hole in the poly flow tubing. Once discovered, it was determined that the poly flow tubing was positioned on the top of the welding machine and vibrations associated with normal runtime had moved it against the exhaust, which with the heat and vibrating against the heat wrap of the exhaust caused a hole in the material. The tubing was fixed and repositioned to prevent contact with the exhaust or elevated temperature components. The platform person in charge (PIC) then provided an all-clear notice and online operations were able to resume. Event Consequences: SMI 128 B Platform was emergency shut down as designed because of the sensor activation. There were no injuries to personnel, property damage, or environmental impacts because of this event. Corrective Action: The following mitigation was taken based on the investigation: 1. The TSE Loop was relocated to the side of the welding machine and secured with tie wraps/zip ties to prevent securing the line in place. Reference Final Report attachment for extended details.

description: While performing routine deck surveillance oily water mixture was noticed leaking from closed drain line on the LP flare header, 4" Pipe in the rack above cellar deck and notified the control room. Oily water mix was noticed, not a gas release. Platform performed a manual ESD and mustered to assess the leak. There were no injuries as a result of muster. Upon further investigation it was the determined that the leak was coming from hole size of 1/8" in the pipe. This led to a calculated volume of 1.96 bbl of fluid of which the composition was 0.99 mole fraction water. All fluids were contained on deck, with no environmental impact to the GOM. Repair plan consisted of installing a plug and allowed to cure for 45 minutes, followed by a 4" clamp shown to have an allowable working pressure up to 150 PSI. The ends of the clamp were wrapped with Belzona 1161 to ensure no seepage. On evening of 12/19/23, the platform began to restore production after a statement of fitness was issued. Please see attached data sheet and photos. Investigation reported will be provided once available. Update 01/12/2024: Below is additional information on the Closed Drain System - including some of the background/historical data and recommendations for going forward. . The LOPC earlier this year (June 23) was at the branch connection for the drain coming from "Sample Sink #2". The defect was identified to primarily be from internal degradation, located immediately opposite/below the incoming flow, and was attributed to an erosion-corrosion or flow-assisted corrosion type mechanism. Temporary repairs were made to this piping and the system was returned to normal operation. . After this LOPC, the PEI Team developed an inspection plan to assess other similar locations. The other locations selected for follow-up NDE were at several branches for Sample Sinks (#s 3, 4, 9, 10, and 11), with the belief that more complex (atypical) chemistry and potential for unusually high corrosion rates may exist at these locations. The inspection of these locations was completed in July in coordination with some additional inspection to assess external degradation associated with coating failure. The lowest measured thickness found was 0.232" at the "Sample Sink #3" location. This was evaluated at the time against the nominal thickness of 0.280" and a start date in 2010 and it was judged that there was not likely an immediate/acute concern with the system. In this sample set the worst measured rate of 3.6 mils/year corrosion rate is effectively the same as the "default" 4 mils/year corrosion rate assumed for many of our systems where erosion-corrosion and/or underdeposit corrosion are anticipated. . The LOPC the morning (December 18) was identified as being at the branch connection coming from the "E" Flow Control Assembly gas vent connection (and was not part of our prior survey sample set). Based on current understanding, the LOPC was likely made apparent during FCA checks on this ESP this morning. The belief is this scenario may be an erosion-corrosion type failure given the potential for relatively high flow rates during the periodic usage of the branches - a slightly different lens than what the team has focused on after this summer's LOPC. Additional RT scope was performed to further understand the overall condition of the closed drain header and ensure better understanding of the degradation mechanisms that may be in play more fully. Investigation report is still ongoing as the team is actively working on gathering all the data. Update 1/26/24: An investigation was not conducted. Please see attached NDE data that shows the inspection drawing used along with what the NDE measurement was, what method was used and date the data was gathered.

description: 12.27.23: The crane operator was using West crane to lower bundle (6 joints of drill pipe) of 5" drill pipe to work boat. The crew had lifted and lowered 62 bundles down to the boat. The boat deck hand and roustabout saw the rigging shifting and immediately moved away to the front of boat clear from the landing zone. The crane was not shock loaded but the crane operator still performed an inspection on crane to ensure there was no damage to crane. Corrective actions: 1. A safety stand down was held. 2. The drill pipe has completions fluid on it so the pipe will be washed prior to being rigged up to increase the friction of the rigging on the bundle. 3. A longer two part sling will be added to reduce the angle and thus the inward pull force when lifting bundle.

description: The crane crew was preparing to lift a tote of xylene from the main deck when as the slings were getting taught, one of the slings got caught under the bolt that tightens down the circular lid of the tote causing the lid to open. description: Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] On 1-18-24 at approximately 2300 hrs. the drill crew was in the process of running a 4 1/2"" production tubing in the hole when the driller slacked off to the connection height and employees set the slips on the tubing. The driller signaled for the derrickman to install the collar clamp; the 3rd party elevator operator thought the driller was signaling him to open the elevators. When the elevators were opened the slips did not hold the string causing the string to slide down inside the slips stopping at the collar. 250' of TEC Line was stressed, & locally damaged at the rotary table and had to be spooled off, re-terminated, and tested. The job was stopped, and leadership notified, the job was started back after a safety pause. A Joint of tubing was screwed into collar and string picked up and collar clamp installed. The tubing that slipped was a new 4.5"" 15.10# S13Cr110 Vam Top. The 1/4"" TEC control line was damaged (control line to the DHPG). The Slips being used were 4.5"" DU long slips configured to be used manually. Estimated cost to repair the 250ft of damaged TEC line is: $1,500. It took 7 hours to make the required TEC re-termination and cut out the damaged portion of the line. No other damages or repairs required and there were no injuries. This is a pending ongoing investigation as corrective measures are still to be determined. Please note this is not a lifting device incident -- the issue was a miscommunication that led to the tubing slipping through the slips without the safety clamp in place. Safety clamps are industry standard when running tubing. The clamps are designed to push down on the slips and make them bite harder if the pipe slips. Pipe slipping through the slips is not an uncommon occurrence in industry when there is not a significant amount of weight below the slips. Per [REDACTED_NAME]'s email, this eWell report is being submitted with the details listed above along with a JSA and photos provided as attachments. Elevator Type or model: Varco BJ 500 ton Elevators

description: On April 4th, 2024, maintenance workers conducted a run test on MTR-0201 (LACT Charge Pump Motor 201) following maintenance activities. During the 30-minute test, it was noted that the motor shaft ceased spinning. Upon checking with the CCR, it was confirmed that the motor was still receiving power (closed contact). Shortly thereafter, workers detected a burning smell. The team had people staged in the MCC Building when starting this pump motor up for the 1st time after a rebuild from the Vendor. {New Bearing on Motor} Smoke was not seen at this time. The workers then started the motor uncoupled from the pump and it ran for about 1 1/2 minutes when they noticed the contactor opened up and the motor stopped. The Electricians smelled some smoke in the MCC. After troubleshooting the Motor Contactor, workers noticed some soot around the Contactor control Circuit components (COIL). Promptly, the CCR was contacted to cut off power to the motor (open contact). No smoke detectors or ICS Muster was activated. Cost of repairs to replace the Motor Contactor Controls (COIL) is around $500. No hot work was being performed and no injuries. During their search, a burnt coil was discovered on the control power circuit for the main contactor on the breaker. It was identified, a small faulty control Transformer was the cause of this incident. No investigation was needed as no work was performed on this motor contactor. This was in service for years. It was just a failed component of a control circuit. The control components and the pump motor has now been in service for days with no issues. See attached photos.

description: Update provided to BSEE OSPD and Lake Jackson District on July 9th, 2024. In accordance with 30 CFR 254.46(b)(2), Williams Oil Gathering LLC hereby submits the following written report regarding a potential oil discharge of greater than one barrel. On June 5th, 2024, Williams Oil Gathering was conducting dewatering/oil filling of the Whale Oil Export Pipeline Segment Number 20556 (ROW OCS-G29496). During the seawater discharge portion of the operation, the ROV, stationed at the seafloor (water depth >8,000 ft) captured what was assumed to be an oily water mix dissipating upward from the water discharge point (AC-730 PLET). As soon as this anomaly was noticed, all flow on the pipeline was halted and by 21:35 no signs of discharge remained visible from the ROV. The flow rate at the time of the assumed oily water discharge was approximately 6.94 BBL/Minute, the discharge lasted from 21:05 to 21:16 placing the discharge total at approximately 76.34 bbls of assumed oily water (a undetermined combination of seawater, mono ethylene glycol, and crude). Any oil reaching the discharge point would have had to bypass 2 slugs of MEG and 3 pipeline pigs to reach the discharge point. The hydrocarbon content at the discharge point is not verifiable and the only possible, potential reference on the actual amount of oil discharged is a sheen spotted in the area (Alaminos Canyon Block 732) by BSEE during an overflight on Friday, June 7th. The sheen was reported to be 9 miles by 3 miles at its widest point, which according to the USCG field ops code, would be consistent with a potential release of 325 gallons or 7.71 bbs.(Witt O'Briens volume estimate attached). Per BSEE OSPD request GE 250G dated June 28th, 2024 Williams is submitting the following information in accordance with 30 CFR 254.46(b) and (NTL) No. 2012 N07: 1. Name of Lessee - Williams Oil Gathering L.L.C. 2. BSEE Operator Code - 02521 3. Point of Contact - [REDACTED_NAME] ([REDACTED_PHONE]) [REDACTED_EMAIL] 4. Description of Initial discharge scenario: a. Structure Type - DOT Pipeline d. Whale Oil Export Pipeline e. Pipeline Segment Number 20556, ROW OCS-G29496 7. Description of the oil Discharged - At the time of the discharge, seawater was being discharged. Any oil discharged would have had to bypass 2 slugs of MEG and 3 pigs. The assumption is that the discharge was a combination of seawater, MEG, and 34.6 API Gravity oil from the Perdido field. 8. The crew then decided not to unload the blasting media from the bulk bag into the hopper, therefore, signaled the crane operator to hoist the bulk bag to set it back down onto the platform deck. Just after the bulk bag was clear of the top of the hopper and the load began to swing, the lift loop failure happened. Once the woven synthetic fiber of the lifting loop/strap broke resulting in the weight of the load shifting, the weight of the load was not equally disbursed. The bag then split open along the seam of the same side of the lifting loop failure causing unspent media to fall onto the hopper and the surrounding solid deck of the platform. The unspent media was contained in the deck and collected manually. Event Consequences: FIBC damage and LOPC. FIBC Cost: $44.00 "Please reference the report within attachments for additional details of the incident investigation. This is a final report submission."

description: Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] On 8/6/24, MPD supervisor requested isolation of "B" choke to clean plugged line for drilling operations. After line was cleaned and "B" choke was reassembled, MPD supervisor requested calibration of "B" choke per procedure MPD-CP-05 while it remained isolated from system. During calibration of "B" choke, the "A" side choke began closing and trapped additional pressure on the well above the planned pressure. The Driller had brought pumps down to prepare for a connection and was only running the boost pump at 90spm at the time of the event. This unexpected closure of "A" choke caused the MPD PRVs on the MPD choke manifold to trip, releasing 4bbls of SBM (BaraECD 12ppg), containing 2.3 barrels of base oil to the overboard diverter line before the choke position was corrected. Investigation is ongoing. Latitude: 28 degrees 08' 10" Longitude: 089 degrees 29' 47" Weather: PARTLY CLOUDY Wind speed: 10 KNTS Current speed: .5 Please see attached SDS Sheet, Choke Plugging procedures, and Hazard Identification Prompt Card. Corrective Actions: The following step is being added to the choke plugging procedure after choke re-assembly. This assumes a Cortec CX4 choke with a position indicator that has a gauge readout. This would also apply to other types of chokes that can have their position externally verified to compare with the Victus display. -Check choke position on the gauge of the choke position indicator and compare to Victus choke position. Place choke in manual while isolated and move open or close by 1%. Verify the isolated choke is the one responding to the command. Check the Victus choke % with the position indicator gauge by functioning choke fully open and fully closed. Victus position and choke indicator should be within 5% of each other. -NOTE: If choke calibration is necessary, both chokes must be isolated before continuing. This will involve bypassing both MPD chokes which may require an assisted shut in. An MOC is required for any deviation. There was no equipment damage, and no cost associated with the equipment.

description: Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] On 12/6/2024 at approximately 0730 hrs., the crane crew was in the process of picking up a bundle of 4 1/2" drill pipe to land on the tubular catwalk. description: On June 22, 2006, Employee #1 was working as a refinery worker at the Kern Oil & Refinery Company just outside Bakersfield, California. He sustained secon d- and third-degree burns over approximately twenty-two percent of his body. The burns were confined primarily to his legs. He was hospitalized. description: Contractor Supervisor: At approximately 3:10pm on May 31, 2021, an automation technician working on the electronics of the #3 Crane, was passing through the upper pedestal (engine area) of Crane #3. As he stepped through the space, fell into an approximately 2.5' diameter hatch (approx 6' deep). Member exited the space through the hatch opening of his own volition. Evaluated by the onsite Medic, who in consultation with an onshore Physician, made the decision to have member sent to shore for further evaluation. There was no apparent life threatening injury. The worker was transported to shore from the facility at approximately 5:30pm via routine helicopter flight. Verbal notification made via NTL RE:reporting clarifications at 5:45pm. Contact made with second number in chart (BSEE). Accepted verbal notification and advised to make entry into eWell. Update 6/1/21: Wood employee taken to clinic for further evaluation. Diagnosed with contusions (bruises) to body and knee. No fractures or lacerations. Given release to return to work at normal duty. Worker requested to return to continue his hitch offshore. First Aid Case. Update 6/2/2021: Dimensions of the accessway into the pedestal of the crane is 22" x 24.5". It is a square accessway, and the space into the pedestal below it is 72" deep (at it's deepest point). At the time of the incident there was approximately 18" of oily water in the bottom of the pedestal space below the accessway. The accessway is used to enter the pedestal for access to crane components/controls. The pedestal space is containment for the engine and accumulates rain water runoff through/from the engine compartment. It is pumped out as a maintenance function as levels of runoff accumulate, based primarily on the frequency, duration and/or intensity of rain. The accessway cover consisted of a section of fiberglass grating that covered the space, which had been cut apart from the adjacent pieces to facilitate removal. The underside of the grating was covered with metal screen to prevent small parts from falling through. It was determined that the dimensions of this section of grating was one inch smaller than the dimension of the accessway. Over time, the metal screen underlayment had bent down and no longer was below the edges of the grating, which further allowed the grating to slide. According to the worker who fell, as member passed through the space and stepped on the grating accessway cover, it slid and fell into/through the accessway. Member fell into the accessway with it. A survey of the other two cranes (of the same design/configuration) found that the grating coverings of the accessways were of sufficient dimensions to prevent the same occurrence. However, as a preventive action, the grating accessway covers of all three cranes were replaced with metal covers of an improved design. The new covers consist of 3"x3"x1/4" angle iron frames with steel grating permanently attached as an inset. The angle iron frames allow the cover to engage the sides of the accessway frame to prevent slippage in any direction. description: Crane operator was preparing to lift wireline equipment onboard the structure, as the lift was initiated the crane engine began to runaway. The Crane engine kill was immediately pulled without success, operator shut crane in with the ESD. Upon engine shutdown it was identified there was a hole in the crane blower case. Crane is currently OOS until repairs are made. This is final report. Please see attached incident investigation. 6/30/2021 - At approximately 0650 hours on Wednesday, June 16th immediately after setting the wireline lubricator onwell, the crane engine made a noise and began to overspeed. At the time of event, the crane operator was in the process of securing the crane. Upon hearing the overspeed pulled the crane engine kill. The engine did not stop so then activated the ESD and the engine stopped. The crane operator then discovered the damage to blower case housing. The crane remained out of service and secured along with the well until crane engine repair was complete. Actions taken to secure the site: . Pressure on casing and tubing was bleed to Zero and the well was full of water . MRBP was set at 7300' MD and tested 1000psi above last know shut in pressure for 30 mins (well is isolated from all producing perforations) . The SCSSV was bled to zero hydraulically, the Lower Master closed, and Crown closed, as well as the wing and wing SDV closed . The lubricator from top of tree through the deck was secured in place with approved tie down devices (chain and binders). Governor and blower assemblies were replaced.

description: A contractor employee was in the process performing hot work to cut a section of 12" pipe on the pipeline skid. In doing so, he was using a 5 foot cutting torch to complete the task. During the cutting on pipe, a flash fire occurred - the fire watch quickly extinguished the fire. The employee cutting was struck by fire on the right side of his face. The employee was stabilized and was transported to shore by crew boat. The employee was taken to a medical facility where they were treated for 1st degree burns to right side of face and released to modified work. Prior to commencing hot work activity, the pipe was checked by opening several needle valves in which clear salt water was discharged. This was a contributing factor to incorrectly consider the line did not contain flammable material. There were two (2) cuts made into the pipe. The 1st cut was made on the lower end of pipe without incident and that it further was an indication that the line did not contain flammables. When the 2nd cut was made on the upper end of the pipe, it caused a flash fire due to due combustible material inside of pipe. description: On a multi-service semi-submersible facility in the Mississippi Canyon area, an incident occured involving the vessel experiencing a power loss, resulting in a vessel blackout. Within 30 seconds back up power generation allowed for control recovery with thrusters available for DP. Vessel was brought back on DP with a minor drift of 1 meter noted. Troubleshooting led to a faulty relay and was repaired. No injuries, no damages. Cause - Troubleshooting found Generator #4 tripped due to an air stop on the fuel system which was caused by a fuel pump failure. The fuel pump was replaced upon discovery. Fault finding into the black ship caused by the Advanced Generator Supervisor (AGS) system was investigated. The AGS had failed to recognize that the #4 gen was experiencing fuel pump problems and remove it from the bus as designed. Findings and corrections: Solenoid valve on Diesel Generator No. 4 was determined to be defective that caused a voltage droop and subsequent reverse power failure on the day of the incident. During this episode the AGS inadvertently tripped the other two diesel generators resulting in momentary black ship. The Manufacturer updated the the AGS protection to include: - "Net voltage to AGS" to 1, to send the net voltage for calculation. - "Inconsistency on delay" from 5 seconds to 10 seconds. This delays the switching of the KVAr signal from measured to calculated. Vessel crew created a pneumatic jig that simulated the previous fault, including the same movement for Kw, fuel rack and frequency. AGS witnessed two tests on Diesel Generator No. 4 and one test on Diesel Generator No 3 with the simulated fault using the updated AGS protection system parameters. AGS was able to correctly identify the healthy generators while tripping the simulated fault generator on reverse power with the ring bus remaining connected. All testing on the AGS protection system completed to satisfaction of attending Surveyor. Note - ABS Survey Report Attached.

As the load of pipe was lowered and approximately 8FT from the supply deck the M/V surged astern. . When the M/V surged astern the load moved towards the M/V and off path of the desired landing area which caused the load to set on the top of a handrail of an aluminum gangway that was stowed near the forward crash rail on the supply deck. . In an effort to prevent further damage; the crane operator began to hoist the load and swing the boom, but the M/V continued to move in reverse causing the load to contact forward crash rail and then the handrails on the cabin of the M/V. . The crane operator continued to swing the boom to get the load free of the M/V's cabin handrails and the M/V stopped reversing and the load was lifted clear of the M/V. . The M/V then established a position where the load could safely be received, and the crane operator placed the load on the supply deck of the vessel without further incident. . Once backloading operations were concluded the crane operator reported the event to the Person-in-Charge (PIC) on the platform and then the Field Foreman and AOL's incident reporting requirements were initiated which included reporting the incident to the Field Foreman, Production Forman, and HSE Coordinator for investigation. Event Consequences 1. Aluminum handrail of portable gangway was bent downward slightly. 2. Surface paint of the M/V was scuffed on the handrails and forward crash rail where contact was made. 3. The insulators keep any metal-to-metal contact from happening, so the interim mitigation is to conduct inspections of the area in normal rounds.

description: Event Description - Sequence / Timeline On April 20th at 12:00HRS during offloading and backloading of the M/V, the crane operator was moving a grocery box on the back deck of the vessel when the grocery box struck a protruding pad eye on an aluminum box that was close to the intended landing area, breaking it off the box. Stop Work was initiated, and the UWA/PIC went down to the vessel to initiate the investigation and gather witness statements. The Field Foreman, Production Foreman, and HSE Coordinator were contacted to report the incident. Event Consequences The aluminum gang box with the broken pad eye remained on the vessel and will be offloaded at the dock upon arrival. The dock was contacted regarding the damage so that they can prepare to safely offload it from the vessel upon arrival and it will be transported back to the owner for repair. There were no injuries or environmental impacts as a result of this event. Please find attached the Incident Report including Root Cause determination and Corrective Action Plan.

description: On 4/26/2023, while preforming the PM on NOV rental generator #1, the termination box was opened and the main conductor leads were observed to be missing insulation, melted, and not connected. No injuries and no environmental impact. Potential causes - Conductor on A phase (L1) got hot enough to melt away from the crimp lug. As soon as that wire melted off, it caused unwanted amperage loads to the other 2 phases, and overheated the wire to their limits, melting them completely off. Both B phase (L2) conductors are completely disconnected from the lugs and weren't touching the bar. This could have happened within 10 to 15 minutes after the first phase melted off, because it trickles down to the weakest link, which were the cheap crimp lugs provided by NOV. New mechanical lugs were installed that will not melt & re-terminated the cables.

description: This is initial eWell and final report. Event The Affected Individual (AI) was getting onto a rigid type of offshore transfer device (OTD) for transfer from the marine vessel (M/V) to the platform and wave action caused the M/V to subside between the wave crest and through approximately 3' from beneath the basket. When the vessel rose back to sea level, the supply deck contacted the underside of the OTD. Event Description - Sequence / Timeline On April 28, 2023, at approximately 07:20HRS, Personnel Transfer Operations were underway between the facility crane and the marine vessel (M/V). . Just prior to the event, the platform crane had lowered the rigid type of offshore transfer device (OTD) to the supply deck of the M/V. The OTD was received by a deckhand of the M/V crew and personnel were offloaded. . On the second transfer, the AI and two other persons were staged to board the OTD and once readied for transfer they would be hoisted onto the platform. o Once the OTD was positioned on the supply deck of the M/V, the affected individual (AI) was the first to board and was, as reported, positioned with one foot on the OTD and his other foot on the deck positioning himself ready for transfer. o Before the other persons could board the basket, the M/V sustained wave action that caused the M/V to subside between the wave create and trough approximately 3' from beneath the OTD, which was then suspended, and when the M/V rose again this caused the supply deck to contact the bottom side of the OTD where it remained close to its original position. o Initially, the AI did not report an injury or conditions of concern following contact between the M/V and the OTD. o The AI remained as he was positioned on the OTD, and the other two persons boarded the OTD. When all parties were safely positioned on the OTD, the crane operator was provided a hoisting signal and they were all hoisted onto the platform. o Once on the platform, the AI began position-related task. . At approximately 09:20HRS, the AI reported discomfort in his right knee to his supervisor and explained what had occurred while he was on the OTD earlier that morning. The person in charge (PIC) of the facility was also informed at this time. o The PIC then reported the AI's condition to Area 5's Field Foreman and AOL's incident reporting requirements were initiated, which included reporting the event to the Area's Production Foreman, and the HSE Coordinator. . At 13:30HRS the AI requested to be sent shoreside for an onshore medical evaluation. . At 16:15HRS an Aircraft departed MP 123 A with an onshore destination. . The AI was transported by their employer to an occupational medical clinic for evaluation, diagnosis, and treatment is needed. . The medical evaluation provided a diagnosis of a knee strain. The AI received a release to regular duty as the condition did not require any medical treatment beyond the initial evaluation and first aid guidance on care. Based on this information, the employer acknowledged that the case was classified as a First Aid. Event Consequences 1. Initially there were no event consequences beyond the contact of the M/V supply deck and rigid offshore transfer device. 2. 2 hours later, a report of discomfort was provided, which required evacuation for medical evaluation, condition diagnosis, and treatment if needed. o Diagnosis: Musculoskeletal Injury/Right Knee Strain There were no environmental impacts or property damages because of this event.

The M/V stopped around 40 feet away from the platform and sent workers in the man basket by crane with fire hoses and fire extinguishers who, by 10 pm, completely extinguish the burning boards. For additional protection a water hose was left on site to continue saturating the boards with water. The workers without harm or injury, safely returned to the barge. Weather: Seas 4 - 6'. description: 10.03.2023: Total costs incurred: ~730,000 USD. 09.29.2023: As per 30 CFR 250.190, Talos ERT LLC respectfully submits the final investigation report (attached) as a follow up to the initial notification of a crane/material handling incident that occurred at SMI-130B on 05.12.2023. 05.22.2023: As required by 30 CFR 250.188 (a)(8); Talos ERT respectfully made verbal notification on 05.12.2023 at 17:00 hours to BSEE of a crane boom failure that occurred at SMI-130B (G02280) on 05.12.2023 at 1605 hours. Incident Details The M/V arrived on location today 05.12.2023 at approximately 14:30. Personnel were offloaded at that time. At approximately 15:00 the platform began preparations to offload construction equipment. Ten lifts were performed (welding machines, bottle racks, toolboxes etc.) were made with the fast line. The eleventh lift was a 3' X 20' grating rack weighing approximately 11,000 lbs and was made with the load line. The platform crane made the lift off the M/V and was approximately 6' off the top deck at a 76-degree boom angle when the boom cable failed. The grating rack fell ~6' onto the top deck and was followed by the boom descending onto the top deck, two connex boxes and the tip rotated over the platform east handrail at its saddle point. See attached pictures for reference. No personnel were in the drop zone or injured in the boom failure. No process piping or equipment was damaged, and no environmental releases occurred. There was significant damage to the crane boom and minor damage to the production deck, conex, and outside handrails. The boom has been properly secured and the area had been barricaded off pending investigation. Talos will follow up with a formal report upon completion of the investigation as required by 30 CFR 250.190. Due to the nature of the incident, crane disassembly, and independent third party failure analysis Talos expects the investigation to take approximately 45 days to complete.

When controls were engaged, the pipe spinner tail end moved away from the IP, then the IP engaged the controls in a reverse direction, causing the pipe spinner tail to move towards the IP resulting in the impact to the hard hat causing it to land on rig floor. Initial Actions Taken: Both Floorhands approached IP to assist him as he was retrieving his hard hat. IP put his hard hat back on and all three moved back into position to continue the task of backing out the drill pipe to rack back in the derrick. Investigation Findings: No malfunction of the pipe spinner was identified. . IP failed to change body position when controls were engaged to change direction of pipe spinner rotation. . IP was standing between the pipe spinner attached to the pipe stand in rotary and the single joint of drill pipe in the mouse hole. . The standard procedure when changing direction of rotation of pipe spinner is to move with the pipe spinner as it rotates and stops when the snub line is tight. . After the pipe spinner was attached to drill pipe, IP operated the pipe spinner to rotate the drill pipe into the drill string in the rotary, IP then waited for driller to give the signal to proceed to back the drill pipe out with the pipe spinner. . The IP did not request any first aid assistance prior to resuming the task of operating the pipe spinner. . 07/04/23 06:30 hrs. IP informed OIM of feeling unwell and was instructed to see medic. (Approximately 15 1/2 hrs post incident). IP was sent onshore at 1:00 a.m. for evaluation by a doctor.

description: At approximately 3:30am on July 12th operators observed the tubing on a vessel tap on the subsea freewater knockout was parted at the fitting from the valve it connects to releasing hydrocarbons. A manual ESD of the FWKO was initiated and the release was secure. The amount released to water is still being determined. The event was reported to NRC, NRC #1372825. Statement 08/25/23: At approximately 3:00 AM on July 12, 2023, Olympus operations discovered a ball valve separation in the sample line between the Subsea FWKO and the sample sink, resulting in a release of hydrocarbons to the deck. Initial spill calculations were made using a tubing flow restriction model. This estimate was based on tubing flow restriction - modeled flow through a 12" inch tube with full pressure drop indicated an 87.78 gallons per minute release rate. At this rate, approximately 31 barrels of hydrocarbon were released to the deck over the 15-minute duration of the event. The initial report to NRC was based on this estimate. The first estimate was later updated because Operations informed the engineer running the calculation that the release did not come through the tubing, but in fact the tubing disconnected during the event, allowing the material to flow from a connection that has a nominal 0.5 inch, inside diameter, orifice. The first model run incorrectly assumed flow through a length of tubing. Consequently, the flow equations for flow from a tube were not appropriate since the tube disconnected. Therefore, a model designed for exit velocity from an orifice was used on the second pass. These model results indicated a choked flow that was limited by the maximum possible flow rate for this scenario. The revised flow rate of 46 gallons per minute, correlating to a 16.4-barrel release to the deck was then reported to the NRC. A sheen on the water was observed during daylight hours. The 0.5 gallon released to water was estimated using a spill estimator, based on the dimensions of the sheen and US Coast Guard spill factors. Operations staff spent the day cleaning spilled material from the bottom deck, where the Subsea FWKO is located, and three decks above due to a significant updraft between the process modules and the well bay. Each deck was cleaned with a combination of absorbent pads, rags, hoses and sprayers.

description: RUE G-23624 At approximately 0700 smoke was observed coming from the main Living quarter laundry room Dryer #4. Power was secured to the dryer and a muster alarm was initiated. The fire team bunkered, and two fire team members partially opened the dryer door and extinguished the smoldering contents in the dryer using a fire extinguisher. No flame was visible when this occurred. YSH 55001A in the area alarmed after muster had been initiated and the door was partially opened to extinguish the smoldering content. Once the smoldering contents were extinguished and cooled, the dryer contents were taken out. This included towels, mop heads, and one oven mitt (see attached photos). The oven mitt was the only item from inside the kitchen area. The load was described as the usual size, but it was noted that another cycle was run on this load because the contents were still wet after the initial drying cycle. This is not common with the dryers and when the smoke was first observed all dryers, including the one where the smoke was coming from had completed their cycle. No indication of lint build-up outside of the normal amount from a load of towels. The dryer vents had been cleaned one month prior. After the dryer was removed the fire damper (FD-5124) appeared to be in the closed position, but the Ruskin fusible link with a rating of 212 Fahrenheit appeared fully intact. The link was not connected to the damper indicating that the damper had been closed without the melted fusible link triggering it per design. No issues with the motor belt on the dryer were found. FINAL INVESTIGATION FINDINGS- Why did the incident happen? FD-5124 is a Ruskin Model DIBD2-WR Fire Damper that is installed on the exhaust ducting in the Main Quarters Laundry Room. The damper pre-maturely failed causing the flaps to Close in the Fail-Safe position. This in turn prevented the dryer from properly venting the hot exhaust air from the dryer. The dryer overheated causing the linen inside to overheat and smolder. The damper was found with the Fusible link lying next to the damper on the floor. The clips that hold the Fusible Link in place were found to be weakened which allowed the Fusible Link to be released from its working position that keeps the flap open. The damper is considered failed and will be replaced with a new one. Additional Action taken since the incident happened: The camp boss will set expectations for crews to stop the job if clothes are still wet after one load and report. If clothes are damp, an extra 10-15 minutes can be added, but will not be set to another full cycle of 45 minutes. Damages did not exceed $25k threshold.

description: Initial notification: (Sept. 10th) at 08:00pm, a crane material handling incident occurred (no injuries) at WD 80D. Current site activity is the Plug and Abandonment of the D-12 well. Crew had picked up a drill collar with 2 7/8" single-joint pipe elevators and set into the slips. Then latched on to a joint of 2 3/8" tubing from the pipe rack and lifted it 6 feet when it released from the single-joint pipe elevators falling back to the pipe rack. All stop was initiated and it was identified that the 2 7/8" single-joint pipe elevators were inadvertently used to hoist the 2 3/8" tubing rather than switching to the 2 3/8" single-joint pipe elevators. description: RUE 23579_x000D_ _x000D_ On January 11th, 2024 a PTL heard an unfamiliar sound coming from turbine generator #3, where it was noticed pulsing on the expansion joint of the exhaust plenum. The largest piece of debris, weighing 44 lbs (20kg), was found on a Southwest laydown area, which is 110ft(33m) drop. Based on the 'Drops' calculator, the outcome could be a potential fatality. description: Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] On 01/08/2024 at 0830 hrs., the task was to remove bolts from the A-4 coflex 8"" flange and replace with new bolts. The original bolts were heavily corroded and rusty. This entailed the cutting of the bolts with a battery operated sawzall. Once the bolts were cut, one worker would use a 10 pounds hammer and a smaller bolt to drive the bottom end of the bolt out of the bolt hole after the top half was removed. At the time of the incident, a second worker (IP) had the left hand under one of the bolts to catch the bottom half of the bolt due to the work being on the 3rd level above the water. Both workers were wearing leather gloves. During the striking of the smaller bolt with the hammer onto the cut bolt, the bottom half bolt came out onto the IP's finger and the momentum drove the hand/finger down onto the flange body. The result was IP's left ring finger that was caught between the old bolt and flange body causing a laceration. IP was taken to the medic where treatment occurred. Upon consulting with the onshore doctor, it was advised that IP be sent in for further evaluation. IP was flown in on 01/08/2024 at 1200 hrs. [REDACTED MEDICAL TREATEMENT TIED TO A SPECIFIC IP] The Hammer weighed approximately 10 pounds, the driving smaller bolt weighed approximately 2 pounds, and the cut half of the old bolt weighed approximately 5 pounds. IP will work light duty starting on 1/9/24 with a 3 to 4 weeks return to normal duty. Please see attached photos and JSA. Update: 01/25/2024 - See attached Early Learning Bulletin.

description: Summary of 01/14/2024 Spurious Trip Event Resulting in PSD and Muster:_x000D_ On 01/14/2024 at 17:11hrs, Thunder Horse had a spurious trip by a line-of-sight Spectrex 900 series detector (AXT-J20215) in the Production Module, resulting in a PSD1 and full muster. AXTJ20215's ESS logic is a 1 activation trip to PSD1. Per the attached PI data, on the day of the event (01/14/2024 at 1711hrs), AXT-J20215 reached 3.133% LEL. The straight signal response indicates a malfunction. This can be compared to the expected curve response generated from a test with a lens on 01/14/2024 at 18:34hrs._x000D_ _x000D_ On 01/15/2024, the detector, including the transmitter, receiver, and HAWK cable gland, was replaced in-kind and put into service. Maintenance reported only slight damage to the HAWK cable gland. The detector that tripped will be sent to SOTEC for RCA to confirm the device failure and determine if the failure may be applicable to devices in the same batch._x000D_ _x000D_ AXT-J20215 was upgraded from a 200 series to a 900 series in June 2022 (MO# 100897642). SOTEC had recently cleaned, calibrated, and aligned the detector on 11/11/2022. At the time, line of sight was verified to be unobstructed, and the device was put back into service. The Crane operator was in the process of lowering the work platform into position when the vessel took an unexpected heave which cause the load to shift unexpectedly. The Banksman observed the load movement and called an all stop to the lift. The Crane Operator was instructed by the Banksman to begin lifting the work platform from the area and return to storage position. When the Crane Operator began to pick the work platform up the momentum caused the work platform to come into contact with a light fixture in the aft end of the Moonpool Area causing minor damage to the fixture and wiring in the area. The work platform was removed from the area without further issue. When the Crane Operator lowered the work platform to the Well Test Deck the load began to move again and came into contact with another light fixture at the forward end of the Well Test Deck causing minor damage to the light fixture. The Crane Operator was able to successfully land the load and reported the issues to their supervisor. The lift into the Moonpool was a blind lift. The lift at the Well Test Deck was not blind lift. At the time of the two incidents everyone was in the proper Safe Step Back Areas or on the tag lines in accordance with the job plan. There were no injuries reported. Crane operator used radio communication. No Dropped Objects were created due to the incident. Estimate repair cost is ~ $600. Please see attached photo, JSA and certificates.

description: Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] The Olympic Challenger subsea crane was being used to deploy a subsea basket. The basket was about 400m off bottom when the Nautilus hook opened and the empty 8x8 basket was lost. The closest subsea infrastructure is approx. 100m away. An All Stop was called and the crane recovered the hook to the surface. An ROV was launched to survey the seafloor in the area and to find the basket. There were no injuries that occurred. The ROV spotted the basket upright in the mud, free of damages. The only damage is to the hook that failed which will cost approximately $300 to repair. The basket will be recovered to deck once all subsea beacons are put in along with installation aids. Please see attached JSA, Certificates, lift plan, and incident report that includes photos. Per Question: How was the hook able to open with weight on it? Answer: The Nautilus ROV hook was found to be defective and locked open. Impacted hook is currently quarantined. Update 02/15/2024: 1. Will there be more information on why the latch was locked open? Did it leave the deck open? It left the deck closed and locked. It appears that at some point the ROV basket heaved and allowed the Nautilus hook to "roll in" the mater link which in turn allowed the monkey's fist to be caught on the master link below which damaged the release pin linkage opening the Nautilus hook. This allowed the basket to drop subsea. 2. Why the hook was found without the monkeys fist and wire loop attached and the pull pin damaged, indicating that it was pulled free under force and the pin subjected to contact? Please see above explanation. It was damaged in a heave of the basket.

description: Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] BA538 Air Compressors/Air Compressor Dryers/Inverter Incident Report On Friday, June 7, the SISC Commissioning team began startup/ testing the platform Air Compressors/Dryers. First, the two Air Compressor Breakers in the AC Panel were closed to supply power to the Air Compressors. Next, the two Dryer breakers were closed, and then the two load contactors were energized from the HMI to supply power to the Dryers. At this point, all conditions were normal, and we were ready to start the air compressors. We first started CBA-80700 and successfully ran it for about 10 minutes, and then sent the start command to start CBA-80710. When CBA-80710 began to start, we heard a loud "humming" noise in the PCE building, started to look around and instantly saw smoke coming out of the Inverter. Upon seeing smoke, we immediately stopped CBA-80710. At this point, we called an all stop to confirm no personnel were injured, opened breakers for all previously mentioned equipment, report the incident, and to start investigating what could have caused this issue. All power feeding into the PCE building was de-energized and LOTO installed so that we could start identifying where the smoke came from within the inverter. After initial inspection, we found a faulted capacitor on one of the circuit boards within the Inverter. Once that faulted capacitor was identified, we continued to inspect the inverter. We were able to find internal factory installed cables (Lout & Nout-PE) with loose connections and there was no antioxidant compound installed on the connections. At this point, we determined the loose connections could have contributed to the inverter failure (pending confirmation from the manufacturer) but kept inspecting the remaining components in the system. We then inspected the AC Panel and megger tested the Air Compressors/Air Compressor Dryers wiring, and all readings were within acceptable tolerances. description: On 06/22/24 at approximately 13:23, the HP Oil Separator (MBD-115) level safety LT-115A was to be tested for the high/low shutdown. The HP oil separator was not in use at the time. An ACR, who has performed this task many times in the past, identified that there was sufficient level in the vessel based on the LT-115A level measurement. They started the testing process by closing the upper vessel isolation valves and opening the needle valve on top of the level bridle. The ball valve that allows gas to flow (bleed) to the skid was slightly opened to allow gas pressure to fall and the level to rise in the bridle by reducing the pressure above the liquid level. The indicated level in the bridle rose faster than expected and the ACR closed the ball valve. The control room operator (CRO) radioed that the high-level shutdown setpoint was not reached and the ACR re-opened the ball valve allowing gas to flow to the skid and allowing the level to rise. Again, the bridle level rose quickly and reached the LSH setpoint. The ACR then proceeded to prepare the draining of the liquids by closing the lower vessel isolation valve and opening the upper vessel isolation valve. Before draining the liquids the ASH-1017 and ASH-1008 detected sufficient gas (2oo45) with 1017 being in "Alarm" (25% LEL) and 1008 at least in "warning" (10% LEL) . This resulted in a platform shutdown (PSD) per the Cause and Effects. The technician performing the check notified the CCR immediately. Note: Gas detectors that came into alarm that then caused shut down, cleared instantly. 11 wells were flowing (in service) during the time of event. No muster was involved because it was known what caused the incident and it was not an ICS event. The cause was due to the Technician bleeding a level bridal too fast causing the volume of gas to make its way to 2 Gas detectors. Since this was a human performance event, coaching was conducted with the individual. There were no damages to the equipment, no injuries, and no hot work being performed.

description: Description of Incident: At 9:37 am, helicopter with a BSEE Inspector onboard approached Platform Edith for a landing and neither the pilot nor the Platform Edith crane operator was aware of the other's presence in the helicopter landing area, creating a potential safety hazard. Using the Flightradar24 application it was determined that during the orbit, the helicopter came around the South side at an approximately 500 feet and then came around far to the North. Using crane engine data provided by Coastline Equipment, the Crane Operator started the engine of the North crane at 9:33am. Edith cranes are equipped with a flashing red light on the crane cab to warn incoming helicopters that the crane is in use and would have been active during the initial helicopter orbit. Based on flight log from Flightradar24 at 9:39 am the pilot was on final approach to land when he saw the crane was in operation and aborted the landing just before passing over the outer fencing on the East side of the helideck and the crane boom approximately 100-feet from the West edge of the helipad. Once the crane operator became aware of the helicopter, he safely completed the lift, parked and secured the crane. The engine data from Coastline Equipment shows the crane engine was shut off at 9:45 am. The pilot safely landed on the helipad at 9:47 am as shown in the flight log from Flightradar24. _x000D_ _x000D_ See attachment for full Incident Report.

description: Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] On 09/27/2024 at approximately 15:30hrs, while in the process of deploying the coflex hose from the MV StimStar3 the crane was hooked to the rigging on the coflex and began the process of taking up the slack in the rigging. description: Contractor Supervisor: [REDACTED_NAME] Incident Title: Wireline Parting / Activation of Upper Shear Ram. Description: While recovering the BHA after the 2nd perforation run on October 24th , at approximately 05:30 am an unexpected increase in tension was noticed by the wireline technician. The wireline crew immediately stopped the wire and called the client representative. Immediate action: The well was shut-in at the choke and PWV/PIV. The grease still was still holding well pressure and there was no release to sea. Multiple meetings were conducted to risk assess options with offshore crews and onshore support. Procedure amendments and clarifications were created to attempt recovery of the BHA into the lubricator. Decision was made to eventually continue with approved overpull to recover the BHA into the lubricator. The BHA was moved up-hole from 6,898-ft (initial stuck point) to 6,512-ft. With 5,900-lbs of tension at 5,612-ft, the wire above the PCH in open water parted, leaving a section in open water connected through the PCH, and down to the BHA. After discussing the status with the leadership team, decision was made to activate the upper shear ram to cut the wire and let the BHA fall to current TD. Additional Information: Upon review, the wire parted at less than half of the maximum tension allowed per procedure. More meetings where scheduled and risk assessments performed. The consensus of the group was to cut the wire with the upper shear ram in the WCP and recover the PCH to surface. Procedural amendments/clarifications were created, and the wire was cut per procedure. The subsea assets were flushed per procedure and the PCH and wire were recovered to deck. At no time during the event was well control compromised, and no wellbore fluids were released to the environment.

If the operator could not get out he cooled slag in the form of a soli d "button," the trackhoe was used to tap the pot to loosen the button and get it to fall out. The coworker checked the first two pots by hand, found them to be cool, and dumped them without incident. He then checked the next two pots by han d, putting the slag hauler between them and climbing out of the cab. He felt the top rim of the two pots and did not sense any heat, so he picked up one of the pots to take it to the dumping area. The dumping area is normally wet from the w ater spray used to cool blister copper slag pots, and from water that accumulate s during storms, snow melt, etc. When this pot was turned upside down, the crust that had formed on the surface broke, allowing molten slag to spill out. After about 10 minutes of inhaling the mist, the employee was coughing and choking uncontrollably and had to leave the room. The employee donned his respirator and returned to the room at which time the exhaust system came back online and removed the mist. Over the next two weeks the employee and fourteen coworkers were sent to clinics to get checked. The doctors that examined the employee and his coworkers were not familiar with the details of the incident, concentrations involved or complications from occupational exposure to chromium and no additional information was made available. The employee's health deteriorated and his blood chrome concentration kept increasing over the next month. On August 16, 2019, he was hospitalized and treated for two days with his final diagnosis still pending.
